bullets: The new PGMem reference implementation turns safety requirements for an agent’s personal memory into executable checks. It includes provenance-typed records, permission-gated assistance, recall thresholds that trigger abstention, execution-time consent checks, 19 automated tests, and a synthetic dataset covering 240 participants and 17,142 task episodes. Why it matters: If you are evaluating assistants that remember sensitive personal information, PGMem offers testable criteria beyond recall accuracy: whether the system can trace evidence, decline unsupported recall, and recheck consent before acting. Its synthetic data does not establish real-world safety, but the implementation can help teams decide whether a memory architecture enforces those behaviors at all. Evidence: E001. High confidence.

The new AmbiGUI benchmark tests whether agents operating graphical user interfaces ask for clarification when an instruction is ambiguous instead of acting immediately. This evaluates a decision boundary that ordinary task-completion scores can miss: recognizing when the requested action is not sufficiently specified. Why it matters: If you are selecting an agent for web pages or applications where a mistaken click can have consequences, AmbiGUI adds a way to compare appropriate hesitation rather than rewarding completion alone. It can separate agents that resolve uncertainty through questions from agents that merely proceed and happen to succeed on fully specified tasks. Evidence: E059. High confidence.

The new leak-reduced DNA benchmark collection provides replacement splits that remove copied, overlapping, or closely related sequences across training and test sets. Its authors report that, in affected tasks, a rule using the label of the most similar training sequence can reach published scores. A separate new study likewise finds substantial label disagreement among some software-vulnerability benchmarks, reinforcing a recurring validity pressure in this captured feed. Why it matters: If you are comparing biological sequence models, using the replacement splits can change whether a score reflects generalization or recognition of near-duplicates. More broadly, the supporting vulnerability study means benchmark choice can change conclusions through incompatible labels, so suite selection may require split-similarity and label-consistency audits before model rankings are treated as comparable. Evidence: E040, E037. High confidence.

The updated VieSign-10K release now distinguishes an original sign-language benchmark that permits signer overlap from VieSign-SI447, whose training, validation, and test partitions contain mutually disjoint signer groups. The latter contains 4,252 videos across 447 sign classes. Why it matters: If you are evaluating sign recognition for unfamiliar people, the signer-independent split tests that deployment condition directly. Results from the overlapping split and the signer-independent split answer different questions, so this update can change which protocol is appropriate and prevent performance on previously seen signers from being mistaken for cross-person generalization. Evidence: E076. High confidence.

The new sampled version of the SRA-50 retrieval benchmark keeps the same 50 runs, 500 queries, and ground truth while reducing the indexed sequences enough to support inexpensive repeated evaluation during training. Its release explicitly warns that absolute scores are not comparable with the full SRA-50 v2 benchmark because removing irrelevant sequences makes retrieval easier. Why it matters: If you need frequent training-time checks, this artifact offers a cheaper proxy while defining a clear comparison boundary. It supports within-run progress tracking, but using its higher scores in a leaderboard against full-benchmark results would create a misleading model comparison. Evidence: E031. High confidence.
bullets_zh: 新的 PGMem 参考实现将智能体个人记忆的安全要求转化为可执行检查。它包括带来源类型的记录、受权限控制的协助、触发拒答的记忆检索阈值、执行时的同意检查、19 项自动化测试，以及覆盖 240 名参与者和 17,142 个任务回合的合成数据集。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估能够记住敏感个人信息的助手，PGMem 提供了超越记忆检索准确率的可测试标准：系统能否追溯证据、拒绝无依据的记忆检索，并在采取行动前重新检查同意状态。其合成数据无法证实真实世界中的安全性，但该实现可以帮助团队判断一种记忆架构是否真正强制执行了这些行为。Evidence: E001. High confidence.

新的 AmbiGUI 基准测试考查操作图形用户界面的智能体在指令含糊时，是否会请求澄清，而不是立即行动。这评估了普通任务完成分数可能忽略的一条决策边界：识别所要求的操作是否没有得到充分说明。Why it matters: 如果你正在为网页或应用程序选择智能体，而一次错误点击可能造成后果，AmbiGUI 提供了一种比较智能体能否适当犹豫的方法，而不只是奖励任务完成。它可以区分通过提问来消除不确定性的智能体与只是继续执行、碰巧在指令完整的任务上取得成功的智能体。Evidence: E059. High confidence.

新的低泄漏 DNA 基准集合提供了替代数据划分，移除了训练集与测试集之间复制、重叠或密切相关的序列。其作者报告称，在受影响的任务中，一条使用最相似训练序列标签的规则即可达到已发表的分数。另一项新的独立研究同样发现，某些软件漏洞基准之间存在大量标签分歧，进一步印证了本次采集信息流中反复出现的有效性压力。Why it matters: 如果你正在比较生物序列模型，使用替代划分可能会改变分数究竟反映泛化能力，还是对近重复样本的识别。更广泛地说，作为支持证据的漏洞研究意味着，基准选择可能因标签不兼容而改变结论，因此在将模型排名视为可比之前，选择评测套件时可能需要审计数据划分的相似性和标签一致性。Evidence: E040, E037. High confidence.

更新后的 VieSign-10K 版本现在明确区分了允许手语者重叠的原始手语基准与 VieSign-SI447；后者的训练、验证和测试分区包含彼此完全不重叠的手语者群体。后者包含 4,252 个视频，涵盖 447 个手语类别。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估针对陌生人的手语识别能力，手语者独立划分可以直接测试这一部署条件。重叠划分与手语者独立划分的结果回答的是不同问题，因此此次更新可能会改变适用的评测协议，并防止把模型在先前见过的手语者上的表现误认为跨个体泛化能力。Evidence: E076. High confidence.

新版 SRA-50 检索基准的采样版本保留了相同的 50 次运行、500 个查询和真实标注，同时充分减少了索引序列的数量，从而支持在训练期间以较低成本反复评估。该版本明确警告，由于移除无关序列会降低检索难度，其绝对分数无法与完整的 SRA-50 v2 基准进行比较。Why it matters: 如果你需要在训练期间频繁检查，这一制品提供了成本更低的代理评测，同时界定了清晰的比较边界。它支持跟踪单次运行内的进展，但如果在排行榜上用其较高分数与完整基准的结果比较，就会造成具有误导性的模型对比。Evidence: E031. High confidence.

evidence_items.summary: PGMem is a Python implementation of a provenance-governed framework for an agentic personal assistant. The assistant is designed for people with mild cognitive impairment, mild dementia or acquired brain injury. The package implements: an evidence-typed personal event base; graduated assistance with permission-gated escalation; threshold-based grounded recall with abstention; consent checks at execution time; the framework's four operating invariants. Nineteen automated tests check the code against the paper's equations, invariants and counterexamples. A synthetic dataset accompanies the code. It contains 240 participants, 17,142 task episodes, 3,081 records and 4,320 recall questions, described by Frictionless Data Package metadata. The metadata supports cohort statistics and validation of real datasets with the same structure. Compared with a reminder app and a single-agent RAG baseline on identical histories, the framework showed: zero invented outcomes and zero fabricated recollections; zero contacts with a trusted person after consent was withdrawn; the lowest false-prompt rate (0.20). In exchange, task success (0.82 vs 0.91) and answer coverage (0.62) were lower. All data are synthetic, so the results illustrate how the rules behave and do not show clinical benefit.
evidence_items.title: PGMem: A Reference Implementation of Provenance-Governed Agentic Memory Support with a Synthetic Dataset and Statistical Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Zero-trust security requires continuous identity verification, but repeated re-authentication creates friction that users work around. This thesis investigates whether keyboard and mouse dynamics can support continuous authentication across three datasets: a primary collection of approximately 30 users (Dataset A), the KMT benchmark of 88 users (Dataset B), and a multi-session dataset of 8 users with 6 to 9 sessions each (Dataset C). The core contribution is mode-aware fusion, which retains single-modality windows rather than discarding any window missing either keyboard or mouse activity. On Dataset C, this recovers 44.5% of usable windows that an inner-join pipeline would drop and keeps three of eight users in scope who would otherwise be unmodeled. Mouse-only authentication on recovered windows reaches EER 0.030 on the strongest user, while keyboard-only authentication fails for six of eight users due to insufficient activity or the limits of character-agnostic free-text features. Cross-dataset transfer between Datasets A and B failed, indicating that per-deployment enrollment is required in production. The system is positioned as a soft signal within a layered zero-trust architecture, not a standalone gate.
evidence_items.title: Multimodal Behavioral Biometrics for Continuous Authentication in Zero-Trust Systems: A Multi-Dataset Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT The rapid advancement of Generative AI (GenAI) creates new opportunities for spatial planning. However, most existing applications focus on macro‐scale overhead perspectives, leaving street‐level visualization constrained by strict physical and spatial fidelity challenges. We introduce a controllable GenAI‐human interactive framework for producing spatially faithful and realistic street‐level imagery that reflects envisioned planning scenarios. Using Large‐scale solar photovoltaic (LSPV) site planning as a test case, it leverages vision‐language models to integrate human inputs (e.g., textual intent, scribbles) and existing status photos, synthesizing photorealistic outcomes. To support systematic evaluation, we constructed a large‐scale street‐view imagery dataset of before‐and‐after solar panel installation across the United States. We comprehensively evaluated 11 model settings covering five open‐sourced diffusion models and one commercial vision foundation model to test fidelity and realism. Our study illustrates how a GenAI‐human interactive pipeline can support visualizing proposed environmental interventions, and offers a benchmark for conditioned GenAI visualization applications.
evidence_items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Planning Scenario Visualization: A Framework and Benchmark for Controllable Street‐Level Image Synthesis

evidence_items.summary: Computer-use agents increasingly handle private information and act on users' behalf across desktop and web applications, including email. Phishing therefore poses privacy and security risks that depend not only on whether agents recognize malicious messages, but also on how they respond. Existing phishing datasets were developed primarily for conventional detection, leaving agent susceptibility to persuasive malicious requests insufficiently characterized. To expose vulnerabilities that pre-existing datasets may miss, we introduce AgentPhishing, a benchmark for evaluating whether persuasive phishing attacks can evade detection and induce LLM email agents to comply with malicious requests. We develop PhishOpt, which optimizes reusable email-generation skills against individual agents under fixed benchmark constraints and a realism constraint. We analyze the generated emails using Cialdini's persuasion principles to identify strategies associated with agent failures and use these findings to construct a universal generation skill. Our evaluation shows that agents can handle pre-existing phishing emails safely yet remain susceptible to attacks adapted to agent behavior, while in an AgentPhishing evaluation of nine agents, four exhibit phishing-detection rates below $10\%$ and malicious-request compliance rates above $45\%$. These results highlight the limits of inferring agent safety from conventional phishing evaluations and the need to assess how agents respond to persuasive malicious requests.
evidence_items.title: AgentPhishing: A Benchmark of LLM Email Agents Under Adaptive Attack

evidence_items.summary: Bashkir is a low-resource agglutinative language written in Cyrillic and remains poorly represented in modern LLMs. We present an open resource suite and a systematic benchmark of adaptation methods: the Bashkir Web Corpus (71,567 documents, 46.9M tokens, 16 sources) and three labelled datasets for binary, multiclass and multilabel text classification; the benchmark covers the first two. Experiments use eight architectures (82M-8B: DistilGPT2, GPT-2 base/medium, Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B, YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B, mBERT, XLM-R) and three adaptation groups (full fine-tuning, QLoRA, in-context learning), plus continual pretraining (CPT). (1) QLoRA on 3.8-8B models outperforms encoder-only fine-tuning on binary classification: YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B with CPT reaches macro-F1 0.748 vs 0.653 (XLM-R) and 0.650 (mBERT); pairwise differences are significant after Holm correction (p<0.001). (2) YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B significantly outperforms Mistral-7B and Phi-3-mini on multiclass classification, BPB and native-speaker ratings (mean 3.28 vs 2.52 and 2.22; n=100; alpha=0.69-0.77; p<0.05); on binary classification its QLoRA advantage is not significant (p>=0.084). (3) CPT effects depend on model and task: perplexity improves for Phi-3-mini (+0.58) and YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B (+0.33) but worsens for Mistral-7B (-1.15, p<0.001); on binary classification CPT helps Mistral-7B most (+4.0 macro-F1). (4) Tokeniser fertility on Bashkir varies 2.67x (2.92-7.80) and tracks adaptation quality, while perplexity across tokenisers is not comparable. Cyrillic tokenisers with Russian pretraining are preferable; LLM judges reproduce native ratings for grammar and coherence (rho=0.33-0.46) but not language correctness (rho=0.16, p=0.11); native evaluation remains necessary. All artefacts are open-licensed.
evidence_items.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Large Language Models to a Low-Resource Agglutinative Language: A Corpus, Datasets, and a Reproducible Benchmark for the Bashkir Language

evidence_items.summary: Training Arabic large language models faces challenges from noisy web data, dialectal variation, and the high cost of continual pretraining (CPT). We introduce AQL-Lite (AQL: Arabic Quality Language), a time- and resource-efficient framework for adapting a multilingual LLM to Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). AQL-Lite couples a quality-first curation pipeline (structural cleaning, heuristic and model-based filtering, MSA selection, and deduplication) with a partial-parameter CPT recipe that trains RS-LoRA adapters across the network together with the last eight transformer blocks and the embedding matrix, under layer-wise learning rates. At a matched 1B-token budget, CPT on AQL-curated data raises a four-benchmark Arabic mean by 3.51 points over CPT on raw web text, which yields no gain over the base model. In a controlled 5B-token comparison, AQL-Lite recovers 94% of the gain of full-parameter CPT (mean 73.19 vs. 73.58) in 52% of the wall-clock time and outperforms adapter-only baselines on every benchmark, and a component ablation shows that adapters, unfrozen blocks, and embedding training each contribute. Scaled to 40B MSA tokens and instruction-tuned on one million examples, the resulting 12B model scores 75.3 on the seven-benchmark Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard v2 (OALL v2) suite. These results suggest that partial-parameter CPT on a carefully curated corpus is a practical route to efficient MSA adaptation.
evidence_items.title: AQL-Lite: Enabling Efficient Knowledge Acquisition for Arabic LLMs via Data-Centric Continual Pretraining

evidence_items.summary: Ophthalmic clinical decision support requires fast, accurate, and privacy-preserving inference, yet autoregressive large language models (LLMs) incur substantial latency and computational overhead for decisions among predefined actions. We therefore investigate a decision-oriented alternative to generative reasoning. Specifically, we first introduce RetiJev-Data, a source-grounded ophthalmology corpus comprising 78,158 clinical-decision and diagnosis questions derived from articles in PubMed Central and a MeSH vocabulary covering 531 eye diseases, and 50,074 guideline-grading questions spanning 11 grading systems, along with a 24,662-question evaluation benchmark. Based on this, we develop RetiJev, a family of 0.8B-9B decision models that directly score candidate answers without autoregressive decoding. Across all model sizes, RetiJev outperforms both a 27B LLM and the commercial Jev 1.13 decision model on guideline grading by 10.4-23.0 points. RetiJev-9B further achieves the highest accuracy on clinical decisions, improving over both baselines by 5.4-6.5 points while matching them on diagnosis. It answers a case in 158 ms on one GPU, 3.5x faster than LLM generation and 470x faster than reasoning. Models are released at https://github.com/Awenbocc/RetiJev.
evidence_items.title: RetiJev: Fast and Source-Grounded Ophthalmic Decision Models

evidence_items.summary: Spatial intelligence requires agents to actively acquire visual evidence and integrate observations into a coherent representation of the three-dimensional world. Yet spatial question answering offers limited evidence of whether models can construct accurate metric maps through autonomous exploration. We introduce SpatialScout, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language model (VLM) agents on active object-level 3D mapping. SpatialScout comprises 80 diverse indoor scenes containing 3,140 target objects. Given an object inventory, RGB observations, camera calibration, and camera poses, agents control a camera to explore each scene and estimate object centers in a shared coordinate frame. The task requires coordinating viewpoint selection, cross-view association, geometric estimation, and map revision under bounded interaction budgets. Evaluation jointly measures localization accuracy and target coverage through object-scale overlap scores that penalize missing predictions. Experiments with frontier VLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated model, Claude Opus 5.5, achieves a mean overlap score of 41.71%, with 47.23% of targets exceeding an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.5 and only 3.25% exceeding 0.9. These results reveal a substantial gap between recovering coarse object layouts and constructing complete, precise metric maps. SpatialScout provides a quantitative testbed for developing agents that build reliable 3D spatial representations through active perception. Code is available at https://github.com/JesseZZZZZ/SpatialScout.
evidence_items.title: SpatialScout: Can VLM Agents Actively Explore and Map 3D Scenes?

evidence_items.summary: The emergence of language-based AI agents promises to transform the scope of machine economic activity. Instead of just proposing bids or following hard-coded protocols, such agents can be used to negotiate and execute agreements in natural language. However, most evaluations of these abilities have focused on one-off exchanges or simple economic games, leaving open the rich space of time-extended, contingent, and incomplete contracts expressible in language; they also focus on raw profit, without measuring the qualities required for trustworthy contracting. We address this by formulating a rational framework for how agents should negotiate and perform natural language contracts in uncertain multi-step environments. Using this framework, we develop metrics and baselines for quantifying rational and cooperative play. We instantiate our framework in ContractSim, an evaluation suite where two players negotiate and execute a multi-turn supplier contract under environmental and inter-player uncertainty. We find that LLM-based agents agree on efficient contracts when environmental uncertainty is low, but under high uncertainty, often fail to negotiate satisfiable, efficient, or mutually beneficial contracts, underperforming even heuristic baselines. When executing contracts, LLM agents are also frequently uncooperative, violating contracts for extra profit even when they are easy to satisfy. These findings highlight room for improvement in the design of language agents that can negotiate and execute contracts both rationally and cooperatively.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Rational Contracting in Natural Language

evidence_items.summary: Automated Text-to-Speech (TTS) evaluation methods (Mean Opinion Score (MOS) predictors and Audio Large Language Model (Audio-LLM) judges) are expected to reflect human perception, yet it is unclear how well they capture the distinct aspects of speech that listeners actually perceive. We deconstruct "naturalness" into a linguistically grounded annotation schema spanning 10 distinct perceptual dimensions, and use it to construct the first dimension-level meta-evaluation benchmark for TTS, comprising 860 utterances annotated by trained linguist raters. Results from benchmarking four MOS predictors and four Audio-LLM judges reveal that MOS predictors are more sensitive to acoustic signal-level properties at the prosodic and paralinguistic levels, while Audio-LLM judges show selective, prompt-dependent detection that favors word-level errors and does not generalize across all dimensions. Neither class reliably captures a breadth of linguistically structured, human-perceptible speech errors. Our dataset, annotation schema, and evaluation code are publicly released to support more targeted and interpretable TTS evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Naturalness: Probing Automated Text-To-Speech Evaluators on Linguistically Grounded Dimensions

evidence_items.summary: This rubric provides researchers with a structured framework to assess whether a dataset is sufficiently prepared for AI/ML applications across seven core domains, with a focus on data quality and reproducibility. Evaluators score specific criteria on a 0–2 scale to generate overall readiness metrics, collaborating with domain experts for highly specialized assessments. The methodology introduces critical "gating" thresholds in areas such as FAIRness, Provenance, Standards, and Ethics, where failing to meet minimum requirements results in an automatic overall evaluation failure. To guide reviewers, the document outlines precise scoring calculations and includes a detailed glossary defining essential infrastructure, ethical, and technical terms. Ultimately, this tool serves as a rigorous checklist to ensure datasets are reliably and ethically prepared for machine learning applications. The rubric accompanies our “AI-readiness Criteria for Biomedical Data,” available at https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.10.23.619844 .
evidence_items.title: Rubric for review of AI-readiness evaluation criteria

evidence_items.summary: Solutions for eight instances of Dataset 2 of the Medical Student Scheduling (MSS) benchmark, each improving the best solution published for its instance. The benchmark is by Zanazzo, Ceschia, Dovier and Schaerf (Journal of Scheduling 28(2):233-246, 2025, DOI 10.1007/s10951-024-00806-z). The problem is a maximisation. Published values are from Table 8 of the paper and match the solution files in the authors' repository, both consulted on 28 September 2026: I40 24 1: 7799 to 7839 I80 12 1: 8614 to 8615 I80 24 1: 16453 to 16455 I160 12 1: 17748 to 17750 I160 24 1: 31470 to 31510 I240 24 1: 50278 to 50291 I320 12 1: 31897 to 31910 I320 24 1: 65943 to 65951 These are feasible solutions. No optimality and no new upper bound are claimed for any of them. Every solution is in the authors' own format and can be checked with the authors' own MiniZinc model (https://bitbucket.org/satt/mss data, Software/Minizinc/mss.mzn) and a public solver: the model accepts each schedule and prints the stated objective. The deposit also contains an independent evaluator written from scratch from that model, calibrated against all 29 published Dataset 2 solutions, with its complete output, the validation logs and SHA-256 digests of every file. Instances, published solutions and the model belong to their authors and are not redistributed here. Author affiliation and other benchmark results: Team Banzai S.L.U. (https://team-banzai.com).

evidence_items.summary: This dataset provides a reproducible benchmark for evaluating lexical retrieval from OCR/HTR transcriptions of postwar Japanese student and social movement materials. Version 1.0.0 contains a 106-page reference corpus, 69 exact-match queries, 475 positive query-page relevance judgments, page-level recognition outputs for 12 experimental conditions, and a standalone Python script reproducing the Stage 3 retrieval metrics. The benchmark was initially developed for the JINMONCOM 2026 study and can also serve as a common evaluation basis for subsequent OCR/HTR research. The reference transcriptions follow the upstream dataset v1.1.0 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21798820), and trained OCR/HTR models are separately available (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23291038). This release preserves the fixed evaluation data used in the original study without revising the underlying transcriptions. Future releases may extend the evaluation conditions or benchmark data, with changes documented separately for reproducibility.

evidence_items.summary: Test dataset and raw evaluation output for a benchmark of MICA (Gyawali, Dhakal & Cheng, Communications Chemistry 2025) against EModelX(+AF), ModelAngelo, CryoAtom and EMProt for atomic protein model building from cryo-EM maps. The test set contains 30 single particle cryo-EM maps (1.95 to 3.92 Å) released in EMDB/PDB in 2026. Every protein chain of at least 30 residues has no more than 25% sequence identity to any PDB entry released before 2026, so none of the benchmarked methods can have been trained on these proteins or close homologs. Entries were deduplicated at 25% identity and sampled with a fixed seed (2026), 10 per size bin. Files: dataset entries.zip (maps, sequences, deposited reference structures, biological assemblies), af3 predictions.zip (AlphaFold Server predictions used as inputs; subject to the AlphaFold Server Output Terms of Use, non-commercial use only), scoring raw outputs.zip (raw US-align and Phenix chain comparison output for every model), code and tables.zip (snapshot of the code repository with selection tables, scores and protocol).

evidence_items.summary: LLMs are increasingly used as AI tutors, yet existing benchmarks overlook the challenging behaviors common among students with learning and behavioral difficulties. We introduce TutorCaseBench, a benchmark that grounds AI-tutor evaluation in qualitative case studies from pedagogy, educational psychology, and special education. Our pipeline converts documented student categories into case-specific scenarios, tutor-student dialogues, and rubrics grounded in source evidence. The benchmark contains 923 dialogues across five challenge types, evaluated through open-ended response generation (1,560 items) and multiple-choice selection (2,537 items). Across 11 state-of-the-art LLMs, even the strongest model satisfies a rubric criterion in only 55.8% of open-ended cases, while models are better at selecting appropriate strategies than generating situated responses. These results reveal a gap between intervention recognition and context-specific adaptation, especially for open-weight models. All data are publicly available at https://github.com/kixlab/TutorCaseBench.
evidence_items.title: TutorCaseBench: A Case-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Tutors in Supporting Students with Challenging Behaviors

evidence_items.summary: Measuring animal distance and motion in metric units underpins abundance estimation, morphometrics, and movement ecology, yet monocular video lacks metric scale and wildlife datasets lack metric ground truth. We present WildDepth 2, extending the synchronized RGB-LiDAR WildDepth dataset in three directions. (i) Imaging radar: 37 RGB-LiDAR-4D-radar sequences (19,716 frames) with per-point Doppler velocity and a measured error budget, to our knowledge the first imaging-radar wildlife recordings. (ii) Benchmarking: a frozen, checksummed hidden test set for RGB-only distance estimation and RGB+sparse-LiDAR depth completion, evaluated separately on animal and background pixels. (iii) Motion and tracking: metric 3D trajectories obtained by lifting 2D tracks using LiDAR, radar, or monocular depth. Across 48,723 animal frames, object-level radar calibration improves monocular depth over scene-level LiDAR calibration without requiring LiDAR at inference (AbsRel 0.120 vs. 0.198), although animal-level LiDAR remains more accurate (0.052). Across 431 tracks, once-per-track radar scaling reduces 3D position error four-fold (2.20 to 0.58 m) and distance-sampling detection-function bias from -13% to -2%, matching once-per-track LiDAR calibration. Transferring radar Doppler onto LiDAR produces motion masks 3.7 times denser than radar alone at 72% precision, reduces moving-animal LiDAR accumulation error by 37%, and estimates radial speed (r = 0.60), albeit with approximately 50% underestimation.
evidence_items.title: WildDepth-v2: A Synchronized RGB--LiDAR--Radar Dataset and Benchmark for Metric Depth, Motion, and Tracking of Wildlife

evidence_items.summary: Purpose This study aims to examine whether large language models (LLMs) can improve tourism demand forecasting accuracy compared to established statistical and machine learning approaches. Design/methodology/approach A systematic out-of-sample comparison is conducted using monthly tourism arrival data from Eurostat for eight European source markets. Benchmarks include optimized seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average (SARIMA), exponential smoothing (ETS), Prophet, Random Forest and seasonal naive models. Three LLM families are evaluated as zero-shot forecasters. Robustness is assessed across a pre-COVID stable period, a future period beyond LLM training cutoffs and an older model test. Findings LLM-based forecasts demonstrate consistent performance advantages over all benchmark models across countries and evaluation periods. In the main post-COVID period, LLMs achieve mean MASE values of 0.67–0.85 compared to 1.56 for ETS, 2.67 for SARIMA, 3.04 for Prophet and 4.32 for Random Forest. The LLM advantage persists in the pre-COVID stable period (LLM MASE 0.85–0.90 vs SARIMA 1.71 and ETS 1.31), indicating that the benefit extends beyond structural-break contexts. Robustness tests using an older LLM model and forecasts for a future period beyond LLM training data indicate that data contamination does not explain the observed performance patterns. Prompt ablation analysis reveals that providing contextual information (country identity and date labels) is the most beneficial design choice, while seasonal and shock hints offer no consistent improvement. Diebold–Mariano tests show directional evidence favoring LLMs in 31 of 32 pairwise comparisons, though limited test sample size (14–23 observations per country) precludes individual-country statistical significance at conventional levels. Research limitations/implications The analysis focuses on monthly national-level arrival data and zero-shot prompting.
evidence_items.title: Tourism demand forecasting in the artificial intelligence era using large language models

evidence_items.summary: LongRS-Bench is a benchmark dataset designed to support long-term temporal understanding and reasoning in remote sensing vision-language models. It is constructed from multi-temporal satellite imagery and annotations derived from SpaceNet 7, SDSU MidWest Flood, and DynamicEarthNet, covering urban construction, flood evolution, and natural land-surface changes.The dataset contains 63,422 question–answer samples organized into four cognitive categories: evolution summarization, anomaly identification, spatial reasoning, and logical prediction. These categories comprise 12 subtasks that assess the understanding of temporal stages, evolution patterns, temporal inconsistencies, spatial changes, and future or missing states. Image sequences contain an average of 12.56 frames and a maximum of 28 frames. A subset of 5,000 samples provides structured reasoning annotations covering visual observation, feature identification, and evidence-based synthesis.The dataset is constructed through spatial and temporal preprocessing, task-specific question and answer generation, automated quality checks, and manual review. It supports supervised fine-tuning and systematic evaluation of remote sensing vision-language models, with an emphasis on integrating evidence across multiple observations to understand geographic evolution processes.
evidence_items.title: LongRS-Bench: A Large-Scale Benchmark Dataset for Long-Term Remote Sensing Cognition and Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Automatic facial emotion recognition is a key tool in applications such as human-computer interaction, emotional monitoring, and AI-assisted educational environments. This study evaluates the performance of three deep learning architectures in classifying facial expressions corresponding to seven basic emotions. A curated dataset of 20,000 images was built by merging and refining multiple public sources. The images were preprocessed using face detection, resizing to 224×224 pixels, and data augmentation techniques to improve generalization. Three models were implemented: a baseline convolutional neural network (CNN) developed from scratch, a pretrained DenseNet121 architecture with fine-tuning, and an optimized version of ResNet50 incorporating LeakyReLU activation, L2 regularization, label smoothing, and progressive fine-tuning. The results show that while the baseline CNN exhibits limitations in accuracy and overfitting, DenseNet121 significantly improves stability, and the optimized ResNet50 achieves the best overall performance, standing out for its generalization capability and computational efficiency. These findings reinforce the effectiveness of combining transfer learning strategies with advanced training and preprocessing techniques in automatic facial emotion recognition. Keywords: Deep learning; Facial emotion recognition; CNN; DenseNet; ResNet; Transfer learning; Data augmentation; Image preprocessing.
evidence_items.title: Comparative Evaluation of CNN, DenseNet121, and Optimized ResNet50 for Facial Emotion Recognition on a Curated Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background: Clinical prediction models are trained on routine care data, and their quality in deployment depends on that data. However, data-quality assessment in healthcare AI remains largely heuristic: practitioners report missingness tables, class-balance ratios, or demographic summaries, but these numbers are not connected to what actually happens to a model trained on the data. A key open question is whether information available before training can flag which dataset conditions will harm a deployed model. Methods: We report an exploratory benchmark of a five-part, task- and target-specific data-quality profile covering: completeness (how much of the data are missing), label noise (how often recorded labels disagree with the true condition), distributional similarity (how far the training population deviates from the population the model will serve), representativeness (how well the training data cover that population), and temporal integrity (whether future information leaks into training records). Each part is an operational proxy, not a validated instrument, and carries an explicit availability state: a part that cannot be measured is reported as “not measured” rather than imputed as perfect. For every dataset condition we train a real model on the possibly corrupted data and measure how much its log-loss and calibration change on held-out patients, rather than asserting a closed-form relationship. We evaluate three cohorts from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV; Sepsis-3, N=2,000; intensive care unit (ICU) mortality, N=3,000; KDIGO-staged acute kidney injury (AKI), N=2,293) under controlled corruptions, and one external multi-institution database (eICU Collaborative Research Database, eICU-CRD; 202 hospitals). Results: Five findings emerge.
evidence_items.title: A Multidimensional Data-Quality Profile for Clinical Prediction: An Exploratory Benchmark in MIMIC-IV and eICU

evidence_items.summary: Phishing and social engineering remain the main routes to fraud against bank customers. Static warnings lose force as users habituate to them. This paper presents APUX-Bank. This paper is a synthetic benchmark for the design and evaluation of adaptive AI-based user experience (UX) models that defend bank customers against phishing. The dataset simulates a four-arm randomized experiment with 2,400 U.S. adult bank customers and 28,800 message decisions across email, SMS, voice and in-app channels. The four arms are a static warning, a rule-based adaptive warning, an AI-adaptive warning and an AI-adaptive warning with an explanation (AI-XAI). The data were generated from a seeded hierarchical logistic model. Its parameters were set from published phishing research. Logistic regression with participant-clustered errors showed that the AI-adaptive design reduced the odds of clicking a phishing message by 48 percent (OR = 0.52, 95% CI [0.45, 0.59]). The AI-XAI design reduced the odds by 56 percent (OR = 0.44, 95% CI [0.39, 0.51]). The benefit was largest for customers with low digital literacy. AI-XAI also raised usability by 6.2 points on the System Usability Scale and lowered false alarms. Trust in the system mediated 41 percent of its effect on phishing reports. The results held across GEE, random-intercept, probit and linear probability models. A parameter recovery test found that 29 of 31 true values fell inside their 95 percent confidence intervals. The data and all Python code are released for teaching, power analysis and method testing Keywords: Phishing, Social Engineering, Adaptive User Experience, Explainable Artificial Intelligence, Banking Security, Synthetic Data, Logistic Regression.
evidence_items.title: Design and evaluation of adaptive AI-based user experience models for mitigating phishing and social engineering attacks in the U.S. banking sector: A data paper with a synthetic benchmark dataset

evidence_items.summary: Knowledge Graph (KG) accuracy assessment is essential for ensuring data quality in downstream applications, yet remains prohibitively expensive due to annotation costs and scale. Large Language Models (LLMs), trained on vast corpora, offer cheap fact validation but remain unreliable as direct accuracy estimators due to hallucinations and knowledge gaps. We propose a novel approach that exploits LLM capabilities without relying on their correctness: using aggregated LLM predictions as stratification signals for sampling-based accuracy estimation. By partitioning KGs into internally homogeneous strata guided by aggregated LLM outputs, we achieve statistically significant cost reductions ranging from 11% to 54% over unstratified and topology-based baselines on real-world KGs. To scale beyond LLM computational constraints, we introduce a knowledge distillation strategy that transfers stratification signals to efficient student models, requiring annotation of only 0.25% of facts while maintaining signal quality. Experiments on six KGs spanning 20M+ triples demonstrate consistent improvements over SotA methods, with statistical guarantees on accuracy estimates.
evidence_items.title: LLMs as Stratification Signals for KG Accuracy Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Adverse event (AE) reporting systems are central to hospital safety monitoring, yet severity classification remains dependent on human review and may be subject to variability among reviewers. Large language models (LLMs) may support more consistent classification of safety reports. Objective To evaluate agreement between a large language model (LLM)-based classification system and adjudicated expert human classifications of adverse event (AE) severity, while characterizing variability in the human classification process. Methods We analyzed 286 adverse event reports from the institutional safety reporting system of a tertiary academic medical center. Two quality and safety experts independently classified each report according to an A–I severity scale aligned with the National Coordinating Council for Medication Error Reporting and Prevention (NCC MERP) framework; disagreements were adjudicated by a third senior reviewer to establish the final human classification. The same reports were processed by a prespecified LLM-based workflow whose configuration was fixed before evaluation, without training, fine-tuning, calibration, or prompt modification on the study dataset; when the workflow generated clarification questions, the recorded responses were used to produce a second classification. Exact agreement with the final human classification was treated as the primary descriptive agreement measure; one-category differences and larger discordances were considered separately. Results Initial exact agreement between the two human reviewers was 65.4% (187/286), with moderate inter-rater reliability (unweighted Cohen’s κ = 0.563; linear weighted κ = 0.740). The final LLM classification exactly matched the final human classification in 140 of 286 cases (49.0%); 125 (43.7%) differed by one category within the prespecified A–E near-match range, and 21 (7.3%) were larger discordances. Linear weighted Cohen’s κ was 0.728 (bootstrap 95% CI, 0.678–0.770).
evidence_items.title: Large language model–based classification of adverse event severity: agreement with final human classification in a single-center study

evidence_items.summary: The Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI), mandatory under MARPOL Annex VI since January 2023, requires existing ships to demonstrate a design-efficiency level that a large share of the conventionally configured fleet cannot meet without intervention. The tools available to evaluate and plan for compliance, however, are limited: certification grade calculators are proprietary and opaque, while academic treatments tend to embed the computation within one-off scenario studies rather than provide a reusable, openly described instrument. This paper presents the development and preliminary verification of an open, single-file, offline capable web based tool for EEXI calculation and compliance screening. The tool implements the attained-EEXI method of IMO Resolution MEPC.333(76) for the twelve applicable ship types, computes the required EEXI and a quantitative compliance verdict, models the engine and shaft power-limitation (EPL/ShaPoLi) regime, and estimates, for non-compliant vessels, the limiting rating that would bring the attained index to the required value. This was developed under the V-Model methodology, which embeds verification and validation as a structural counterpart of each design stage. Software verification and external validation are reported separately. For verification, two independently written implementations of the governing equations agreed to machine precision (ε ≤ 10⁻¹² %) across a thirteen-vessel matrix of hypothetical test cases spanning ship types, sizes, regulatory boundaries, and the power-limitation regime, and the inverse solver converged to the intended root; this establishes internal consistency of the encoding, not regulatory correctness. For external evidence, the outputs are compared with a published worked example (≈0.2 % deviation) and found to be consistent with an established commercial calculator and with the peer-reviewed literature.

evidence_items.summary: Coding-agent benchmarks often describe a task in natural language but grade it with tests taken from the upstream project. Passing those tests can require information the description never states: a constant's name, a module path, an exact message. We call this a specification-oracle gap: where it exists, a benchmark also measures whether an agent reproduces upstream implementation details. We formalise the gap, including the inconsistencies that chains of dependent tasks add, and build a static audit for five languages that classifies every name-, path- and literal-level dependency of every scored test (held-out precision 89.2%, recall 92.9%). On SWE-Milestone (98 graded milestones, 35 published runs), 25 milestones contain a test that depends on an unstated, non-inferable name or path. Build units with such a dependency fail in 80.6% of runs, against 48.4% for comparable units without one, and withholding a single hidden name from the reference stops its unit's tests from compiling in 126 of 128 cases. The leaderboard's ranking is robust to removing the affected tests, but they shift scores within repositories and favour agents that reproduce upstream names. Across four further benchmarks, prevalence appears to follow construction: a third or more of the tasks are affected where specifications are release notes or LLM summaries, almost none where tasks are screened or written for their tests; how much a gap costs depends on how the harness grades. We release the audit, corrected filter lists and specification addenda.
evidence_items.title: What the Specification Did Not Say: Specification-Oracle Gaps in Test-Graded Coding-Agent Benchmarks

evidence_items.summary: Model fusion aims to integrate the capabilities of multi-expert models into a single model. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage of reasoning with long chains of thought and tool use, while strong average performance can mask substantial losses in individual expert capabilities. We introduce FusionEval, a benchmark that provides controlled expert pools, integrates fusion methods with and without additional training, and offers a unified evaluation suite. The pools contain domain experts independently trained from Qwen3 and Llama base models across math, code, science, instruction following, and tool use. The suite evaluates capability retention and computational cost on eight public benchmarks under comparable data access rules, reporting normalized average and worst performance, runtime, and peak GPU memory usage. Extensive experiments show that training-free methods preserve reasoning performance but substantially degrade tool use at both model scales. In contrast, MOPD preserves tool use and achieves a more balanced capability profile, but requires additional data preparation, inference, and training. Jointly retaining reasoning, instruction following, and tool use at low computational cost remains a challenge. We hope FusionEval supports future research on efficient model fusion that jointly preserves expert capabilities. Our code is available at https://github.com/Baicaihaochi/FusionEval_Benchmark.
evidence_items.title: FusionEval: Benchmarking Model Fusion for Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Automatic phenotype information extraction plays an important role in rare disease diagnosis, genotype-phenotype analysis, and precision medicine. However, accurately identifying phenotype concepts and determining their associations with specific patients remain challenging, particularly in full-text biomedical articles involving multiple patients and complex clinical descriptions. This paper presents an overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1, which aims to promote the development of methods for patient-specific phenotype concept recognition from full-text biomedical literature. The task consists of two subtasks: full-text phenotype concept recognition and patient-specific phenotype association. For this evaluation, we used 200 annotated full-text biomedical articles from the PatientPheX dataset, containing 506 patients, 15,193 phenotype mentions, and 5,656 patient-phenotype associations. A total of 455 teams registered for the competition, with 189 and 103 valid submissions received on the Phase A and Phase B leaderboards, respectively. The best-performing system achieved an overall score of 0.7389 on the final test set, outperforming the baseline by 8.37 percentage points. The top-performing teams explored diverse approaches combining biomedical language models, large language models (LLMs), and ensemble strategies. The evaluation results highlight both the potential of these approaches and the remaining challenges in patient attribution and phenotype normalization from full-text biomedical literature. The post-evaluation phase remains open at https://tianchi.aliyun.com/competition/entrance/532512.
evidence_items.title: Overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1: Patient-Specific Phenotype Concept Recognition in Full-Text Biomedical Literature

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that plan, remember, call tools, coordinate with other agents and act over long horizons with limited supervision. Evidence on whether such agents work reliably is scattered and sometimes contradictory, and recent reviews largely describe architectures, benchmarks or threats in isolation. This systematic, taxonomy-driven critical review follows PRISMA 2020 reporting where applicable, without meta-analytic pooling, and synthesises 98 verified sources published up to 30 June 2026. It differs from prior reviews in four ways. First, it weighs evidence: eight headline claims are graded by an explicit rule, and contradictions are traced to moderators such as feedback source, equal-compute comparison and task verifiability. Second, it specifies a closed-loop reference framework operationally, adding a verification stage and a safety-and-authorisation gate, and codes ten published systems against it; none fully implements both control stages. Third, it links capabilities to evaluation hooks, readiness levels and re-assurance triggers for agents that change after deployment. Fourth, its evidence base is auditable through re-executed searches with measured recall, verified references and a released evidence matrix. High-confidence findings are that intrinsic self-correction is unreliable, long-horizon autonomous planning remains weak and tool-using agents are broadly vulnerable to injection. Multi-agent benefits are conditional (moderate confidence), whereas claims about benchmark validity and memory consistency rest mainly on preprints. A reliability model quantifies the value of independent verification, and an eighteen-direction roadmap is ranked by an explicit priority rule.

evidence_items.summary: Nepali-English code-switched conversational speech presents severe challenges for automatic speech recognition (ASR), chiefly through script confusion (inappropriate mixing of Devanagari and Latin orthography) and elevated error rates at language switch points. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can adapt multilingual foundation models, but human code-switched audio is expensive to collect and annotate. We curate a new benchmark of 13,044 spontaneous podcast utterances (15.45 h total; 10,214 test, 2,830 dev), audited and verified to eliminate machine translation leakages and acoustic loops. We investigate a two-stage synthetic-to-real adaptation framework: Stage 1 applies SFT on 0.95 h of speech synthesized via a multi-speaker, dual-engine TTS pipeline; Stage 2 explores Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with transcription and script rewards. We find that synthetic SFT provides the primary cross-domain transfer to spontaneous human speech, reducing Mixed Error Rate (MER) from 23.40% to 21.52% (-1.88 pp) and switch-point error rate (SPER) from 35.89% to 28.77% (-7.12 pp). Subsequent GRPO yields small, statistically significant adjustments on 173 test utterances (1.69%), driving English script confusion (SCR_en) from 6.45% to 6.36% (p <= 0.001) and SPER to 28.70% (p = 0.022 clustered). Crucially, ablation reveals that in this SFT-converged encoder-decoder setting, an auxiliary script reward term yields performance identical to MER-only optimization because rollout candidate groups exhibit near-zero script variance on synthetic data. On monolingual benchmarks, SFT improves Nepali MER by 2.71 pp (stabilizing at 18.42% after GRPO, a 2.38 pp gain over baseline) while preserving English lexical WER (3.38% vs. 3.33%). Verified transcripts, timestamps, episode metadata, and reconstruction scripts are publicly released.
evidence_items.title: Synthetic-to-Real Code-Switched ASR: A Spontaneous Nepali-English Podcast Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Ambiguity is a central feature of natural communication: a sentence, image, or sound may remain underspecified until evidence from the other channels is considered. Yet current multimodal benchmarks mostly test perception, recognition, or reasoning over already determinate inputs, leaving unclear whether omni-modal large language models can resolve ambiguity distributed across text, vision, and audio. We introduce TRIAD, a benchmark for omni-modal ambiguity resolution. Each item is a text--image--audio triplet paired with a question and a set of answer options, and is constructed so that the full triplet determines a unique answer while removing any one modality makes the set of consistent options non-unique. TRIAD contains $327$ hand-written queries in $86$ scene groups and covers $18$ ambiguity categories across the three modalities. Evaluating $14$ omni-modal systems reveals that strong item-level performance does not translate into robust scene-level disambiguation: the best model still trails humans by over $20$ points in group accuracy. Removing answer options widens the gap further, driving model group accuracy to the single digits while humans remain robust. Leave-one-out and transcript/description counterfactuals further show that current systems often underuse audio cues when text and image are present. TRIAD reframes omni-modal evaluation around disambiguation rather than recognition, and provides a taxonomy, benchmark, and diagnostic protocol for measuring this capability.
evidence_items.title: TRIAD: Benchmarking Omni-Modal Ambiguity in Multimodal Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: We present Protegrity-PII, a new PII decision model for structured and unstructured text. Protegrity-PII achieves a typed recall of 0.915 with a precision of 0.907 on a new benchmark we propose, PII-SCOPE. Our model processes text in 0.49 seconds per million characters at \$0.0005 per million characters on a single RTX 6000 using batched inference. Due in part to the expansive nature of the entity type taxonomy used in training, Protegrity-PII achieves superior out-of-distribution generalization when benchmarked against a selection of state of the art models and datasets.
evidence_items.title: Protegrity-PII Technical Report

evidence_items.summary: Unified audio models capable of audio understanding, audio generation and, increasingly, audio editing are proliferating rapidly. However, each capability is evaluated in isolation on specialized benchmarks and a basic question remains unanswered: can these models understand the audio they generate/edit i.e. do they exhibit audio understanding-generation self-coherence (UGC_OWN)? We introduce TORUS, an audio-native unified benchmark for holistic, closed-loop evaluation of unified audio models comprising 1,053 questions (117 tests) spanning 21 tasks and 8 audio domain settings across all 3 audio types. We evaluate unified models and cascades of specialized models across objective and subjective metrics. Best unified models are able to answer only 52.4% questions about their generations, while gpt-audio can answer 53.6% questions. We hypothesize that a truly unified audio intelligence should be highly self-coherent and thus position understanding-generation coherence as an essential test for future unified audio systems. Further details are on our project page: https://torus-benchmark.github.io/
evidence_items.title: TORUS: A Unified Closed-Loop Benchmark for Unified Audio Models

evidence_items.summary: Ensuring the safety of Large Language Models (LLMs) is critical for real-world deployment. However, current safety measures often fail to address implicit, domain-specific risks. To investigate this gap, we introduce a dataset of 3,000 annotated queries spanning education, finance, and management. Evaluations across 14 leading LLMs reveal a concerning vulnerability: an average jailbreak success rate of 57.8\%. In response, we propose MENTOR, a metacognition-driven self-evolution framework. MENTOR performs metacognitive self-assessment, using strategies such as perspective-taking and consequential reasoning to uncover latent model misalignments. MENTOR couples single-pass rule-guided inference for routine requests with a selectively invoked metacognitive evolution cycle that revises residual unsafe responses, distills successful corrections into a dynamic rule graph, and compiles validated rules into activation-level steering signals for future inference. Experiments demonstrate that MENTOR substantially reduces attack success rates across all tested domains and outperforms existing safety alignment methods. The code and dataset for MENTOR are available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MENTOR-Evo.
evidence_items.title: MENTOR: A Metacognition-Driven Self-Evolution Framework for Uncovering and Mitigating Implicit Domain Risks in LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Most contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems are released with frozen parameters and improve through external updates, whereas an ideal system would keep improving from its own experience, a capacity we call recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet studying RSI requires an environment that is continuously changing, objectively verifiable, and naturally grounded, posing a fundamental challenge for agent evolution. Here we introduce EvoForesight, a sustainable evolution agent system grounded in future event prediction, in which agents continuously interact with a dynamically evolving environment and improve by internalizing and externalizing the experience gained through these interactions. A living environment synthesizes verifiable tasks, and a recursive-evolution engine turns the reasoning trajectory behind each prediction back into capability: decoupling search from prediction adapts parameter-level evolution to the contamination-prone live environment, while distilling reusable skills lets the agent evolve from the limited live trajectories such an environment affords. On the external FutureX leaderboard, which evaluates predictions against real-world outcomes and is updated weekly, our self-improved forecaster ranked first across all systems over three consecutive weeks, achieving up to a 195% improvement in rating. On our synthesized evaluation, it ranked among the top three across four base LLMs, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 10.7 Bradley--Terry points. More broadly, these results suggest that a system built for self-improvement is best understood as an agent that co-evolves with a genuinely living, open-ended environment, pointing to a shift in AI from training static models on fixed data toward cultivating agents that grow stronger from their own experience, with such an open world as the indispensable basis of that growth.
evidence_items.title: Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: AI systems may miss indirect, culturally situated distress or provide support mismatched to the application context. Existing benchmarks do not jointly address cultural variation, application context, and practitioner disagreement. We introduce VEILED-SH, a benchmark and construction methodology for evaluating single-turn responses to indirect expressions of suicide, self-harm, and distress. Its 10,003 prompts span counselor chat, forum posts, platform search, and triage, drawing on Singapore-grounded sources and public datasets. An expert-validated multi-label taxonomy distinguishes intent, communicative function, and response behavior. Six automated profiles, individually calibrated to three peer-support practitioners and three clinicians, retain separate reference policies for proxy-alignment scoring. Evaluating five systems on a coverage-enriched sample reveals variation in proxy alignment across profile-generated reference policies, even for the same system responses.
evidence_items.title: VEILED-SH: Vulnerability Expression through Indirect Language Evaluation Dataset (Self-Harm)

evidence_items.summary: Benchmark scores often misrepresent a large language model's (LLM's) knowledge, because they rely, e.g., on the model's ability to follow specific formatting requirements. This especially penalizes base models that may know the correct answers but lack the ability -- typically introduced in post-training -- to structure them as instructed. To overcome this, we propose an efficient, automated, and architecture-agnostic method for model evaluation based on soft-prompt tuning. By optimizing only 10 soft-prompt vectors (~0.0006% parameters for a 7B model) over a short tuning period, we adapt models to specific benchmark formats, closing gaps in format-following and ensuring that underlying knowledge is accurately reflected in benchmark scores. We evaluate soft-prompt tuning across 7 models and 11 datasets. Our results show that (a) soft-prompt tuning saturates format-following within 150 steps (~1200 samples) while preserving knowledge accuracy, (b) it closely matches strong evaluation-harness baselines on well-studied benchmarks while requiring no manual benchmark-specific prompt or parser design, (c) it improves evaluation signal in settings where baselines are harder to transfer, including long-context datasets and instruction-tuned variants with different output styles, and (d) it produces cleaner outputs that improve agreement between exact match scoring and independent LLM judges. Overall, we propose a lightweight, automated, and flexible protocol based on limited-budget soft-prompt tuning for evaluating LLM knowledge.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Prompt and Parser Engineering: Soft-Prompt Tuning for Automated LLM Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: DC-CoolTwin started as a workaround. We wanted to study how AI workloads, cooling water and cyberattacks affect each other in a data center, but there was no public dataset with all three on the same system. People usually use water-plant or industrial control data instead. We decided to simulate a data center ourselves. The dataset has four sites: Chittagong, Phoenix, Dublin and Singapore. Their climates are very different, which matters a lot for cooling water. Each site has 30 days of one-minute data (43,200 rows). Server load comes from real LLM traffic logs (BurstGPT, Azure 2024) and the weather is real too, from Open-Meteo. The simulator turns that into server heat, chiller and pump behavior, and cooling-tower water loss. We also attacked it. Seven attack types run for roughly 6% of the time: a fake temperature reading, a lowered set-point, replayed old data, a stuck water-level sensor, a drain valve forced open, and a network break-in that ends with tampered cooling settings. Besides 24 sensor columns and the attack labels, there's a column called water wasted L. It shows how much extra water each attack cost, compared with the same run without the attack. Water balance error is under 0.01%, and WUE stays between 1.77 and 2.55 L/kWh, close to real data centers. It should be useful for attack detection, adversarial testing, water forecasting, federated learning and cooling optimization. See README.txt for the columns.
evidence_items.title: DC-CoolTwin: A Physics-Based Digital-Twin Benchmark Dataset of AI Workload, Cooling-Water Consumption, and Cyber-Physical Attacks in Data-Center Cooling Systems

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Short‐term temperature forecasts are useful in many IoT systems, but the models behind them are usually tested on one large public dataset rather than on the cheap sensors actually deployed. We ran one forecasting pipeline—a naive “no change” baseline and three machine‐learning models (Ridge regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost) over lagged and rolling features—on two sources: the Jena Climate benchmark (Germany, 2009–2016, about 420 000 records) and 1 month of data from each of three low‐cost optical particle‐counter nodes in Tetovo, North Macedonia. All splits were chronological, and every evaluation was repeated with walk‐forward cross‐validation. Two of the three field nodes came close to the benchmark in absolute error (RMSE 0.76°C and 0.78°C, against 0.63°C on Jena) on roughly one hundredth of the training data, and two exported two‐feature models ran in real time on an Arduino MKR1000. The rest of the results were less comfortable. At one of those two nodes, no trained model beat the naive baseline, and walk‐forward evaluation showed the tree ensembles there to be far more unstable than the single split suggested. The third node's much larger error was not a modeling failure: its housing was heating in the sun, which we traced in the raw files and the site operators confirmed. Two further data‐quality defects, one per dataset, each changed a reported error figure. On this evidence, a benchmark score on its own says rather little about how a forecasting pipeline will behave on cheap edge hardware in the field.
evidence_items.title: Temperature Forecasting on Low‐Cost Sensor Nodes: What a Public Benchmark Does Not Tell You

evidence_items.summary: This dataset supports the research project: "Design and Development of a Geographic Information System for Fire Service Gap Analysis Based on Isochrone Maps in DKI Jakarta" . It provides a comprehensive collection of spatial and analytical data used to identify fire service "blank spots" and optimize station distribution in a megacity context. The repository contains the following components: Analytical Datasets: Provided in both English (EN) and Indonesian (ID) formats, including administrative boundaries, fire station coordinates (174 active stations), and historical fire incident data (2024-2025). Spatial Map Layers: A .zip archive containing GeoJSON of merged isochrone polygons (4, 5, and 7-minute thresholds) and identified blank spot areas. Spatial Computation Scripts & Database Schema : A dedicated .sql script containing the database Table DDL and Azure SQL Stored Procedures ( spatial analysis pipeline.sql ). This script details the exact spatial logic used for multi-polygon union aggregation ( geometry::UnionAggregate ), intersection calculation ( STIntersection ), unserved blank spot extraction ( STDifference ), metric surface area scaling, and Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) priority scoring. Technical Architecture Diagrams: Detailed visualizations of the system's Backend API (REST), Spatial Database Logic (Azure SQL), and the AI-LLM (Gemini 2.5 Flash) orchestration workflow. User Acceptance Testing (UAT): Raw responses and calculation analysis from 10 diverse professional respondents, validating the system's usability and clarity.

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning research on software vulnerability detection measures progress against a small set of public benchmark datasets, treated as a shared yardstick for comparing models. This approach rests on the untested premise that benchmarks agree: if two datasets have the same function, they give it the same label. We test this assumption by comparing four popular C and C++ benchmarks against one another on their complete data. Label agreement is a symmetric relation, but its strength is uneven. The two benchmarks that derive labels from CVE-linked fixing commits disagree on only 0.68% of 75,019 shared functions, whereas a third disagrees with them on 51.21% and 41.28%. Leakage, in contrast, is directed: we identify 1083 instances in which training data from one benchmark reappears in test data from another, with different counts in each direction. A manual check of 30 contradictory functions traces the disagreements to commit-level labeling and to treating functions left unchanged by a fix as safe. The costs are asymmetric: contradictory labels impair training only slightly, while up to 3.12% of a test set carries a contradicted label, shifting measured accuracy by up to two points. Therefore, reported accuracy reflects both model capabilities and benchmark selection.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Cross-Benchmark Investigation of Label Consistency and Reliability in AI-Based Software Vulnerability Detection

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can perform a broad range of tasks across diverse settings, yet their performance in agentic contexts remains poorly understood. Although online evaluations in simulators and real-world environments are essential for measuring interactive agent performance, they are costly and challenging to scale. Complementary offline VQA benchmarks can enable faster and more reliable comparisons across agentic domains, yet existing benchmarks remain limited and fragmented. To address this gap, we introduce AgentVQA, an offline benchmark for evaluating VLMs on realistic agentic scenarios across five agent domains: Web Agents, Robotics, Egocentric Videos, Games, and Spatial Planning. We build AgentVQA by manually selecting 1000 challenging, real-world agent examples from 23 source datasets and adapting them for reliable offline evaluation. The resulting benchmark preserves realistic scenarios from interactive environments across diverse domains, and its model rankings track those from corresponding online evaluations. Across the 22 evaluated models, the best achieves only 58.5% accuracy. Our cross-domain analysis shows that errors are driven primarily by failures to ground and maintain accurate representations of the current and evolving visual state, including localizing relevant UI elements, interpreting motion, tracking state changes over time, and inferring 3D spatial relationships, rather than by task misinterpretation or downstream logical reasoning.
evidence_items.title: AgentVQA: A Unified Benchmark for Agentic Visual Understanding

evidence_items.summary: In this paper, we introduce GutHub, a comprehensive extraction pipeline developed for the CLEF 2026 GutBrainIE task, addressing Named Entity Recognition (NER), Named Entity Disambiguation (NERD), and Relation Extraction at both the mention (M-RE) and concept (C-RE) levels. The primary obstacle in this domain is navigating extreme class imbalances across a multi-tiered training corpus that ranges from massive, noisy auto-generated text to sparse, expert-curated data. To overcome this, GutHub employs a stacked transformer ensemble combining domain-specific and zero-shot models to mitigate label bias. For disambiguation, SapBERT dense retrieval paired with a Mini-LM reranker trained on the MS-MARCO dataset outperformed several domain-specific alternatives. For mention-level relation extraction we combined class-specific confidence thresholding, deterministic heuristic pruning, and negative sampling. We then mapped the mention-level relations to unique URIs to output the concept-level relations. On the official test set, the micro-F1 scores achieved for each subtask were 0.7893 (NER), 0.3497 (NERD), 0.4029 (M-RE) and 0.1295 (C-RE).
evidence_items.title: GutHub: Tackling the GutBrainIE Task Through Entity Recognition, Disambiguation, and Relation Extraction

evidence_items.summary: Agentic AI systems pursue goals through multi-step planning, tool use, memory, and adaptive action, creating governance challenges that differ from those associated with conventional predictive or generative AI. This study systematically reviews governance evidence relevant to agentic AI in Africa and develops an Ubuntu-informed conceptual framework. Following PRISMA 2020, 91 records published from 2019 to April 2026 were analysed through quantitative content analysis and abductive thematic synthesis. The corpus comprises 12 agentic-AI-specific records, 3 agentic-adjacent records, and 76 broader AI-governance records used as contextual evidence. Five literature-derived gaps were identified: accountability across autonomous action chains, infrastructure-aware oversight, bias and representational harm, policy fragmentation, and community exclusion. These findings inform five proposed governance elements: communal impact assessment, collective consent and participation, infrastructure-contingent oversight, African dataset and bias auditing, and communal accountability. The framework is a literature-derived conceptual proposition, not an empirically validated governance instrument, and requires future case-study, expert-panel, and comparative policy testing.
evidence_items.title: Governing Agentic AI in Africa: A Systematic Literature Review of Ethical Challenges, Framework Gaps, and Ubuntu-Informed Governance Solutions

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for Building Information Modeling (BIM) work, yet published evaluations test one or two models on a single task using simplified inputs, leaving practitioners without an evidence base for choosing between them. This paper’s contribution is a four-track benchmark of ten current models run inside one commercial Revit add-in suite on the production workloads of a working BIM department: requirement extraction from a live ISO 19650 BIM Execution Plan; rule extraction from an 88-page scanned Arabic building code; multimodal drawing review with live application programming interface (API) access, adjudicated and reconciled by two practitioners; and ten colloquial prompts executed in Revit, each carrying an adversarial probe. Scoring combines itemized rubrics, human verification, cross-model consensus and file forensics with telemetry from 218 logged calls. Three models form a leading group, Claude Opus 5 at 88.7 of 100, GPT 5.6 Sol at 86.2 and Claude Fable 5 at 84.7. Neither re-weighting the composite 20,000 times nor repeating the agentic track displaces that group or moves a composite by more than 1.8 points, but the separation inside it is smaller than that variation, so no ordering inside the group is claimed. On these prompts fuzzy name resolution, not code generation, accounts for 60 percent of agentic points lost, which argues for guardrails enforced in the tool layer rather than assumed from model behavior.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Production BIM Workflows Using Agentic Automation

evidence_items.summary: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common neurodegenerative disorder, and its pathology accumulates for years before symptoms appear, which places the mild cognitive impairment (MCI) stage at the centre of early detection. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) applied to structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) report high classification accuracy, yet these figures are usually measured within a single cohort and are rarely tested for transfer to an independent cohort, so whether they translate into clinical usefulness remains unresolved. The objective of this study is to address that gap directly. Six classifiers, three classical learners (Extra Trees, LightGBM and CatBoost) and three deep networks (ConvNeXt, CoAtNet and an introduced bidirectional Vision Mamba model, MambAD) were trained and tested on identical hippocampal slices from three publicly available datasets, namely ADNI, OASIS and a public Kaggle collection, for the three-class staging of cognitively normal (CN), MCI and AD. Every model was evaluated within cohorts and, more importantly, across cohorts, with subject-level scoring on the two clinical datasets. Within the primary ADNI cohort, the introduced model reached the highest balanced accuracy (BAC) at 0.578, although this lead was not statistically significant; across the six models, none dominated on every task, and no pairwise difference between models reached significance. BAC fell from about 0.55 within-cohort to between 0.38 and 0.45 across cohorts for every model, and the deep models transferred better on the ranking metric than the classical learners. The results show that a lightweight state-space model can match far larger pretrained backbones under matched conditions, and they confirm that single cohort accuracy overstates readiness, with cross-dataset generalisation remaining the binding constraint on clinical use.
evidence_items.title: Cross-Dataset Generalisation of Machine Learning and Deep Learning for Three-Class Alzheimer’s Disease Staging: A Six-Model Benchmark Including a Bidirectional State-Space Model

evidence_items.summary: Context: Multi-agent systems built on large language models now plan, call tools and execute code in production settings. Benchmarks measure what such agents can do, and separate efforts measure robustness to prompt injection, but no standard measures whether the orchestration platform that runs them is deployable: whether it terminates, behaves consistently, recovers from faults and enforces governance controls. Objective: We propose AgentGov-Bench, a benchmark that scores a deployed multi-agent platform on four separately reported axes (capability, reliability, governance and cost) and treats governance as eight behavioural invariants to be tested, not as features to be listed. Method: We define the invariants, a test procedure and pass criterion for each, a reliability protocol and a non-fungible deployability profile, and a reference architecture whose components map one-to-one to the invariants. As preliminary evidence we audited the official documentation of five widely used open-source frameworks against the invariants. Results: All five document bounded termination and human-in-the-loop approval as built-in features. None documents per-agent identity as a built-in feature; three offer it through an integration or hosted service. Built-in sandboxed code execution is documented by one framework. The documentation also records conditions under which controls fail open or do not cover all tool types. Conclusion: Feature availability does not establish enforcement. Deployability must be measured on the configured system with behavioural tests, which AgentGov-Bench specifies.
evidence_items.title: From Feature Lists to Enforced Invariants: AgentGov-Bench, a Deployability Benchmark for Multi-Agent LLM Orchestration Platforms

evidence_items.summary: This study legally evaluates the normative synchronization of concurrent government affairs under Law No. 23/2014 regarding the governance of Fishing Vessel Crews (AKP) and formulates an ideal decentralization model. The research method employs normative legal research through statutory and conceptual approaches, focusing the analysis on the harmonization of regulatory texts. The results indicate a regulatory disconnect within Law No. 23/2014, which only divides property-based aspects (in rem) such as vessels and marine zoning, while failing to integrate the protection of its legal subjects (in personam). The centralization of certification and document legalization authority by the central government creates a legal antinomy and a vacuum of supervisory authority at the regional level. This research recommends a legal reconstruction by strengthening functional asymmetric decentralization norms, optimizing the Co-Administration scheme for the Governor, institutionally reconstructing the Syahbandar at regional ports, and establishing local regulations based on data digitalization to achieve legal certainty.
