evidence_items.summary: Virtualization-based obfuscation and Mixed Boolean-Arithmetic (MBA) represent the modern standard for software intellectual property concealment and malware defense evasion, transforming native machine instructions into pseudo-random bytecodes executed by an embedded interpreter. Existing deobfuscation paradigms remain fundamentally brittle: dynamic execution tracing achieves incomplete path coverage while triggering anti-analysis defenses; classical Dynamic Symbolic Execution (DSE) suffers from catastrophic path explosion and prohibitive SMT solver latency over modular bit-vector arithmetic; and virtual stack mechanics leave hundreds of dead operations that overwhelm industry decompilers. In this paper, we present AETHER-64, a fully automated, static bytecode-driven devirtualization and algebraic simplification framework engineered specifically for 64-bit protected binaries. AETHER-64 introduces three foundational innovations: (1) Local-Context Handler Symbolic Slicing, which reconstructs complete Control-Flow Graphs (CFGs) through isolated basic block emulation without accumulating global path constraints; (2) a bit-parallel Algebraic Pre-Reduction (APR) filter grounded in Boolean conjunction lattice signatures and fast Moebius inversion over Z/2^64, resolving invariant dispatch conditions in O(1) time; and (3) syntax-directed I/O-guided non-linear MBA synthesis coupled with LLVM Static Single Assignment (SSA) virtual stack elimination. We evaluate AETHER-64 on the Quarkslab Diffing Obfuscation Dataset (104 ground-truth functions across MiniLua, Zlib, and SQLite comprising 56,883 bytecode instructions), 1,000 synthetic Tigress virtual machines, commercial protections (VMProtect 3.4/3.5, Themida 3.1), and 7-layer non-linear MBA expressions.
evidence_items.title: AETHER-64: High-Throughput Binary Devirtualization via Bit-Parallel Algebraic Pre-Reduction and SSA Bytecode Promotion

evidence_items.summary: Geothermal resource development involves heterogeneous geological and engineering records, uncertain reservoir parameters, and decisions constrained by physical processes and safety requirements. This narrative and critical review examines how large language models (LLMs), including retrieval-augmented and tool-assisted systems, could support knowledge-intensive tasks throughout geothermal exploration, development, and operation. It distinguishes direct geothermal evidence from empirical evaluations in adjacent fields and from conceptual proposals; results from petroleum engineering, mineral exploration, and broader energy systems are not treated as proof of geothermal performance. Peer-reviewed studies demonstrate useful capabilities in technical document extraction, domain question answering, knowledge-graph reasoning, and interactions with scientific software, but direct geothermal engineering validation remains limited. For reservoir inversion, drilling-risk warning, and design optimization, quantitative assessment must rely on measured data and validated physical or numerical models, with LLMs acting as auditable interfaces and information-integration tools. The review proposes a task-specific benchmark framework and examines cross-domain transfer, multimodal alignment, knowledge-graph and retrieval collaboration, uncertainty quantification, and LLM–physical-model coupling. These frameworks are literature-informed proposals rather than implemented geothermal systems. Key priorities include independent geothermal test sets, expert-annotated reference answers, calibrated uncertainty, physics-based verification, and transparent reporting of model failure. The resulting synthesis identifies credible current applications and the evidence requirements for reliable future deployment.
evidence_items.title: From Data to Decision-Making: A Review of Large Language Model Applications Across the Full Lifecycle of Geothermal Resource Development

evidence_items.summary: Decentralized knowledge marketplaces often face an irreconcilable trilemma: Confidentiality (preventing unauthorized scraping and intellectual property theft), Verifiability (enabling decentralized peers to inspect and validate accuracy), and Incentive Alignment (preventing Sybil cartels and collusion). Pure cryptographic zero-knowledge systems conceal data entirely, rendering qualitative peer review impossible; conversely, plaintext crowdsourcing models leak IP to the public, destroying creation incentives. In this paper, we propose  EduChain , a dual cryptographic and game-theoretic framework that resolves this trilemma. EduChain couples a Poseidon-based zk-SNARK authorship commitment scheme with an On-Chain Conditional Key Escrow governed by a novel Review Bond Staking Rollover protocol. To eliminate collusion and reviewer-author bribery, we design a Verifiable Random Assignment (VRA) mechanism parameterized by an on-chain entropy beacon, bounding the cartel hijacking probability to O(1 / C(M, k)). Furthermore, we prove that under our non-inflationary 70/20/10 purchase settlement model, wash-trading cartels face a guaranteed negative-sum capital depletion rate of -10% per transaction, proving that honest participation forms a strict subgame perfect Nash equilibrium. We deploy and benchmark EduChain on an EVM Layer-2 environment. Experimental evaluations across 83 continuous integration test vectors demonstrate that our Groth16 verification requires only 256,160 gas (~$0.006 on Arbitrum/Base) and client-side proof generation completes in under 820 ms, establishing EduChain as a practical, mathematically secure paradigm for decentralized intellectual property evaluation.
evidence_items.title: EduChain: Collusion-Resistant and Confidential Peer Review for Academic Content via Zero-Knowledge Proofs and Stochastic Mechanism Design

evidence_items.summary: This narrative review examines large language model (LLM) assistance with archaeological literature, code, metadata, and transcription, together with the ethical, legal, and governance conditions on its use. I propose a Zotero Model Context Protocol (MCP) citation-review sequence that records the publication version, source evidence, provisional assessment, and review status. A small case study tests source reading with sixty constructed claims about ten randomly selected papers cited in this manuscript. Ten model-and-reasoning configurations assessed the claims against my human reference judgments. Exact label agreement ranged from 80.0% to 100.0%, with nine configurations matching at least 58 of sixty labels. One evaluator reported the correct source values but selected the wrong label; a matching label could also accompany an inadequate page locator. The study used a controlled PDF interface, one human reviewer, and one run per configuration, and did not test the full Zotero workflow. I recommend establishing permission to process research materials and checking outputs against inspectable evidence. LLM-supplied citations require human source review; citations selected through the author’s own reading can receive an LLM audit, with human follow-up on disagreements, unresolved support, and proposed changes.

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence workloads and cloud services require increasingly sophisticated resource allocation, yet conventional scheduling policies may optimize utilization or response time without explicitly accounting for energy consumption and carbon intensity. This paper proposes a Green Artificial Intelligence framework for intelligent resource management that combines workload prediction, energy-aware optimization, service-level constraints, and runtime feedback. The framework estimates near-term demand from system telemetry and selects resource allocations that balance performance, energy use, and operational cost. A carbon-aware objective can incorporate time-varying grid carbon intensity where trustworthy data are available. The proposed evaluation uses trace-driven experiments and a reproducible comparison against static allocation, utilization-based autoscaling, and energy-unaware scheduling. Key measures include energy per completed task, average and tail latency, SLA violation rate, resource utilization, and estimated carbon emissions. A public cloud workload trace and a documented power-measurement model are recommended for implementation in Python. Because no implementation, trace processing, or experiments have been executed for this manuscript, all quantitative results are left pending.
evidence_items.title: GREEN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR INTELLIGENT RESOURCE MANAGEMENT

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by the public and healthcare professionals for clinical reasoning. However, they were developed as general-purpose language models rather than dedicated clinical decision-support tools, and their performance in real-world acute heart failure (AHF) management remains insufficiently evaluated. We compared four contemporary AI models with physician decision-making. Methods This single-center retrospective observational study incorporated a cross-sectional AI evaluation of consecutive patients treated at Sotiria General Hospital between July and November 2025, excluding acute coronary syndrome. ChatGPT, ChatGPT Plus, DeepSeek, and an ESC guideline-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) model independently assessed identical standardized cases. Recommendations were compared with physician decisions on diagnosis, treatment, guideline-directed medical therapy, timing, and prognosis using Cohen’s kappa, McNemar’s test, Cochran’s Q, Wilcoxon signed-rank testing, and multivariable logistic regression. Results Diagnostic performance differed significantly across systems (Cochran’s Q=8.477, P=0.037). In the balanced diagnostic cohort, ChatGPT Plus achieved the highest HF accuracy (accuracy 86.5%; sensitivity 87.0%, specificity 86.0%), followed by RAG (accuracy 77.5%), ChatGPT (accuracy 77.0%), and DeepSeek (accuracy 69.0%). For HF within the top three differential diagnoses, sensitivity was 90.0–97.0%; specificity was 70.0% for ChatGPT Plus, 68.0% for RAG, 19.0% for DeepSeek, and 15.0% for ChatGPT. Physician agreement was highest for guideline-directed therapies, with greater variability in prognosis and escalation of care. RAG more closely matched physician therapeutic timing but did not consistently outperform general-purpose models.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Versus Physician Decision-Making in Acute Heart Failure: A Comparative Evaluation of Four Contemporary AI Systems

evidence_items.summary: Many language-model pipelines end in a closed-set decision, such as selecting a tool. Prompting a large language model for it is slow and order-sensitive. We ask how small an encoder for such decisions can be and whether it should read the options jointly or separately. In a three-seed study at 32 million parameters, per-option scoring beats joint scoring on a held-out sample of a 37-benchmark decision suite by 5.8 points of chance-corrected skill at matched optimizer steps and by 2.8 at approximately matched training compute; two external benchmarks agree, though not significantly on their unseen tasks. Crossing reader with initialisation shows that the advantage requires a reranker initialisation, whose query-candidate pair input matches per-option reading; from the raw encoder the two readers are indistinguishable. Per-option scoring needs 5 to 13 times more encoder passes: at most twice the median latency, but more than four times the mean. Of six released joint encoders (17 million to 1 billion parameters), the 68- and 150-million-parameter models exceed a 435-million-parameter DeBERTa-v3 zero-shot classifier by 4.9 and 5.9 accuracy points on 209 overlap-audited System1-Arena tasks and are at least on par with it on the 145 tasks unseen in training. The smallest answers a median request in 14 milliseconds on 16 processor threads, against 728 for the classifier. Reordering options changes 12 to 23% of the joint models' answers (per-option scoring: none). Up to 68 million parameters, they lead their size range on a public leaderboard's private, mainly in-distribution tests.
evidence_items.title: Joint or Per-Option? Compact Encoders for Closed-Set Decisions from 17 Million to 1 Billion Parameters

evidence_items.summary: Language-model agents acquire capability along two routes that published work almost always varies together, one enlarging the computation a single agent performs and the other enlarging the number of agents and the channels along which they pass partial results, which leaves the contribution of each route indistinguishable. This paper separates an agent system into a reasoning operator and an interaction topology, holding the number of agents fixed at three across all multi-agent topologies, together with the number of rounds, the message cap, the prompt skeleton, and the memory settings for all combinations, and evaluates a full factorial design of four reasoning levels and four topologies on three public test sets totalling 484 instances under five random seeds, giving 38,720 task executions. Comparisons are paired at the instance level, and effects are estimated from logistic mixed-effects models fitted to each test set separately. The reasoning factor spans 18.0 points on the static suite whereas the topology factor spans 7.8 points on the interactive one, a reversal indicating that the two mechanisms act on different failure modes. The topology span is taken across all four topology levels and therefore includes the step from one agent to three, against a structure-only span of 2.8 points among the multi-agent topologies. The two factors also depart from additivity in a localised manner. A mechanism-motivated single-degree-of-freedom contrast on the only cell in which both factors contribute a corrective pass is significant at p = 0.001 on the static suite, whereas the omnibus nine-degree-of-freedom interaction test is not (p = 0.094), and in that cell the observed 50.0 percent lies 5.8 points below the additive expectation. After tokens are counted, seven of the sixteen configurations remain undominated on the static suite and five on the operating-system suite, and returns saturate at 12,400 tokens per instance on the static suite under the present design.
evidence_items.title: Autonomous Agents Based on Large Language Models: Reasoning Strategies and Multi-Agent Interaction

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Assisted reproductive technology (ART) management relies on hormone measurements whose review requires integration of cycle stage, treatment regimen, medication context, and longitudinal hormone history. Manual review demands specialist expertise and sustained attention, potentially limiting efficiency and consistency at high testing volumes. We developed NovaMind, a task-specific large language model (LLM) for patient-level plausibility review of ART hormone results, and explored patient-based real-time quality control (PBRTQC) for complementary system-level monitoring. Methods This study included 5,852 patients and 10,526 review units. Retrospective data collected from 21 May 2020 to 28 February 2026 were partitioned by patient for model development and internal evaluation. NovaMind underwent two-stage supervised fine-tuning and was evaluated against an expert-derived reference standard. Input ablation assessed the contribution of longitudinal hormone history. Prospective evaluation from 1 March to 1 May 2026 included 1,435 consecutive review units in a silent cohort and a challenge set comprising 900 real-world negative units and 100 data-augmented abnormal units. PBRTQC was evaluated using simulated shifts in retrospective data and operated silently on prospective result streams. Results In the internal test set, NovaMind reduced the false-negative rate (FNR) by 11.00 percentage points and increased the negative predictive value (NPV) by 10.30 percentage points compared with conventional autoverification. Adding longitudinal hormone history reduced the FNR from 30.00% to 21.00% and increased the NPV from 90.51% to 93.46%. In the challenge set, NovaMind detected 77 of 100 data-augmented abnormal units and correctly classified 705 of 900 real-world negative units. All 1,435 units in the prospective silent cohort were reference-negative, among which NovaMind achieved 81.95% specificity (95% CI, 79.88%–83.85%).
evidence_items.title: A longitudinally informed large language model for patient-level review of hormone test results in assisted reproductive technology: development, internal testing, and prospective silent evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Advancements in large language models (LLMs) offer opportunities for automating challenging and time-intensive Knowledge Engineering (KE) tasks. Constructing an ontology is particularly complex when modeling logical axioms, especially among novice knowledge engineers and domain experts with limited KE training. Consequently, ontologies often contain modeling errors, undermining ontology-based applications and hindering subsequent KE tasks. Thus, it is important to investigate how LLMs can support KE tasks such as the evaluation of ontologies. However, systematically evaluating LLM performance remains challenging due to a lack of comprehensive, task-specific benchmarks needed for such LLM capability assessments. As a result, selecting the right LLM to support knowledge engineers is nontrivial. This study investigates how LLMs can support four concrete ontology evaluation subtasks: detection, classification, explanation, and possible correction of modeling issues, focusing on the use of existential, universal, and cardinality property restrictions. We construct a benchmark of student-built ontologies and assess the performance of four LLMs—GPT-4o, ClaudeSonnet, DeepSeekV3, and Llama3.3—on these KE subtasks. Additionally, we exemplify an annotation framework for qualitatively evaluating LLM outputs and analyse the capabilities of each model. Our findings reveal differences in model behavior and task-specific strengths, underscoring the importance of selecting an appropriate model for each KE task.
evidence_items.title: Knowledge Engineering With Large Language Models: A Capability Assessment in Evaluating Ontology Property Restrictions

evidence_items.summary: The intelligent transformation of industrial robots is extending inspection from conventional mechanical-performance tests to the evaluation of perception, decision-making, learning, and human–robot interaction. This review summarizes artificial intelligence (AI)-driven robot inspection from two complementary perspectives. First, AI is examined as an inspection tool for appearance-defect recognition, visual trajectory measurement, anomaly detection, online health assessment, and remaining-useful-life prediction, with attention to lightweight and edge-deployment techniques. Second, AI-enabled intelligence is treated as the inspection target, covering visual and force perception, autonomous planning, robustness to distribution shifts, continual-learning stability, and collaborative behavior. The principal obstacles to production deployment are then analyzed, including scarce and imbalanced data, insufficient cross-model generalization, false alarms, real-time constraints, limited interpretability, and the absence of standardized datasets and model-validation procedures. Future research should emphasize inspection-specific efficient architectures, physics–data hybrid models, explainable evidence chains, multimodal foundation models, and lifecycle-oriented standards. These developments are necessary to convert laboratory accuracy into reliable, reproducible, and certifiable performance in industrial environments.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence-driven inspection technologies for industrial robots

evidence_items.summary: Abstract As modern systems evolve into complex microservices and highly regulated data ecosystems, manual test case design has become a severe bottleneck in Agile CI/CD pipelines. While Artificial Intelligence (AI) accelerates code synthesis, standard Generative AI models persistently struggle with the "Oracle Problem." They treat test generation as a stateless translation task, lacking the strategic reasoning necessary to navigate multi-layered industrial requirements without hallucinating logic. To bridge this massive "Design Gap," we propose the Agentic-QA Fusion Framework. This stateful, multi-stage architecture transforms automated test generation into an active reasoning ecosystem. Utilizing a specialized "actor-critic" loop comprising Parser, Triage, Architect, Writer, and Auditor agents, the framework autonomously strategizes, generates, and self-heals test scripts. The framework’s cross-industry scalability is empirically evaluated against baseline ML and deterministic LLMs across five complex datasets. This includes baseline commercial platforms (ISIS Travel, Travco Travel, Vantage Towers) and two highly constrained domains: the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) FIRDS system (requiring strict ISO 20022 messaging) and a governmental Job Matching Platform (JMP). By shifting the focus upstream to cognitive requirement analysis, the proposed framework successfully parses deeply nested regulatory logic. It drastically reduces hallucination and redundancy rates to 1.3% and 7.8%, respectively. Furthermore, it guarantees near-perfect syntactic correctness (99.6%) and achieves an industry-leading Mutation Score of 93.4%. Ultimately, while this Agentic approach necessitates higher computational resources to resolve dense enterprise dependencies, it establishes a reliable, zero-touch automation solution vital for modern software quality engineering.
evidence_items.title: AI-Driven Automation of Software Testing to Enhance Software Quality and Enable Agentic AI

evidence_items.summary: We introduce CARTE (Culturally Anchored Regional-Territorial Evaluation), a multiple-choice benchmark for evaluating the ability of large language models (LLMs) to discriminate fine grained, geographically grounded and regionally differentiated knowledge within France. While prior benchmarks focus on national-level cultural understanding, they largely overlook intra-country variation and the need to distinguish between closely related regional contexts. CARTE addresses this gap by introducing 3,132 questions spanning the 13 metropolitan regions of France and covering 12 thematic domains, including culture, language, demographics, economy, environment, and mobility. Questions underwent four-stage validation: human review, LLM-as-a-judge, model-based difficulty calibration, and a second human review. We further introduce CARTE-LV, a subset targeting Linguistic Variation across French regions, enabling focused evaluation of language-related differences. We evaluate 32 open-weight LLMs of 1B to 30B parameters and three frontier API models across zero-, one-, and three-shot settings. Our experiments reveal performance disparities across regions and model scales, suggesting systematic gaps in pretraining coverage and limited robustness to intra-national variation.
evidence_items.title: CARTE: A Benchmark for Mapping Language Model Knowledge Across France

evidence_items.summary: The identification and localization of errors is a core task in peer review, yet the exponential growth of scientific output has made it increasingly difficult for human reviewers to reliably detect errors given the limited pool of experts. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have sparked interest in their potential to support such evaluation tasks, from academic peer review to automated scientific assessment. However, despite the growing use of LLMs in review systems, their capabilities to pinpoint errors remain underexplored. In this work, we introduce Fault Localization Across Writing in Science (FLAWS), an automated benchmark consisting of 713 paper-error pairs designed to evaluate how effectively LLMs detect errors that undermine key claims in research papers. We construct the benchmark by systematically inserting claim-invalidating errors into peer-reviewed papers using LLMs, paired with an automated evaluation metric that measures whether models can identify and localize these errors. Developing such a benchmark presents unique challenges that we overcome: ensuring that the inserted errors are well-defined, challenging, and relevant to the content of the paper, avoiding artifacts that would make identification trivial, and designing a scalable, automated evaluation metric. On the resulting benchmark, we evaluate five frontier LLMs: Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek Reasoner v3.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT 5, and Grok 4. Among these, GPT 5 is the top-performing model, achieving 39.1% identification accuracy when k=10, where k is the number of top-ranked error text candidates generated by the LLM.
evidence_items.title: FLAWS: A Benchmark for Error Identification and Localization in Scientific Papers

evidence_items.summary: Conformance vectors for agent execution evidence, and the reference verifier that judges them. This release carries 39 corpus manifests across 38 suites and 2,154 vectors in all, among them the in-toto adversarial-execution-evidence predicate, the in-toto ai-agent-action predicate, an AI generation predicate, the observed-effect predicate, SCITT COSE carriage, signed decision receipts and receipt chains, an anchor-stream verifier, ACS core, artifact binding, MCP response-phase interception, the OWASP MCP verification draft, the W3C per-check reporting format and intake, A2A agent-card canonicalization, delegation lifecycle, authority at dispatch, done contracts and receipts, grader isolation, spoofed tool output, test tampering, and ACI deployments. One binary judges every one of them, selected by the suite each corpus manifest declares. Each corpus digest is listed, recomputed from the vector files, in CORPUS-DIGESTS.txt, which the GitHub release signs and timestamps. The predicate's model is execute-and-attest rather than match-and-assert: a consumer recomputes the outcome from the bytes the statement carries, instead of trusting a verdict the producer asserted about itself. This repository is a second, independently usable implementation of that contract, so that any producer of the predicate type can self-certify and any consumer can reject a lying emitter. For the adversarial-execution-evidence corpus this deposit covers suite revision 32: 288 vectors, of which 63 accept, 223 reject and 2 are indeterminate. Its bytes are fixed by the corpus digest bf3e5befd71640757ff1b3f0af63507364b823b5e3f9059678f72f64a46e11c1 recorded in vectors/MANIFEST.json. A published revision is never mutated in place; a normative change to the predicate, or an addition to the corpus, bumps the revision and regenerates every vector byte-identically from its generators, because the vendored specification's digest is itself a corpus input.

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains the experimental datasets, analysis-ready files, and reproducible R workflows generated during the development and characterization of an instant whey–pineapple beverage powder produced by spray drying. The dataset includes the physicochemical characterization of independent cheese-whey batches and Caqueteña pineapple (Ananas comosus (L.) Merr.) pulp, spray-drying processing conditions and responses, physicochemical and technological properties of the resulting powders, and panelist-level sensory acceptance data for the reconstituted beverages. Measured variables include pH, titratable acidity, density, fat or lipid content, protein, moisture content, ash, water activity, °Brix, color coordinates (L , a , and b ), powder yield, solubility, wettability, and hedonic scores for appearance, color, aroma, body, acidity, and characteristic pineapple flavor. The repository provides the original Excel workbooks together with CSV copies of the corresponding data tables to facilitate interoperability. It also includes R scripts for descriptive statistics, statistical comparison of whey batches, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of whey characterization, spray-drying responses, and sensory data, as well as generation of the sensory summaries, heatmap, and manuscript figures. An additional R runner script allows the main analytical workflows and graphical outputs to be reproduced sequentially. A README and detailed data dictionary document the files, worksheets, variables, units, wet- and dry-basis conventions, categorical codes, missing-value conventions, and replicate structure. Together, these resources provide a transparent and reproducible dataset for reuse in spray-drying research, dairy–fruit powder characterization, sensory analysis, and multivariate data analysis.

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous research agents are increasingly used to automate large portions of scientific research, yet they are prone to research integrity violations (RIVs): behaviors that compromise the validity, reproducibility, or faithfulness of the research process. We present RIDAR, a framework for automated RIV detection and runtime intervention. First, we introduce RIVT, a comprehensive taxonomy of 14 RIV types spanning the full research lifecycle. Building on RIVT, we present RIDAR-post-hoc, a framework to detect RIVs within agent trajectories. RIDAR-post-hoc achieves 85.2% F1 performance on RIV-Gold, a benchmark for RIV detection with 60 expert-annotated trajectories. Applying RIDAR-post-hoc to RIV-Wild, a dataset of 300 agent trajectories across 50 distinct research tasks, we detect 3,964 RIV instances in 99.7% of trajectories, revealing the prevalence of RIVs in current agents. Finally, we present RIDAR-runtime, a framework for dynamically detecting and correcting RIVs during agent runtime. RIDAR-runtime effectively reduces agent RIVs remaining at task completion by 36.8%. We will release our code and data to facilitate future research.
evidence_items.title: RIDAR: Safeguarding Research Integrity in Autonomous Research Agents via Automated Detection and Runtime Intervention

evidence_items.summary:
AI coding agents can now build small playable games in minutes, but the results usually look like programmer art: gray blockouts, colored geometric primitives, and flat semantic blobs. We present AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns such footage into high-quality visuals with characters, motion detail, and effects. Throughout, it keeps the layout, camera, and every entity's position and timing intact.
  Our AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres that agents build, such as tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, and crowd runners.
  AnyGameRenderer takes plain video as its game-state input, with no complex representations such as engine G-buffers, per-object class labels, or low-poly proxies. Gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, and wireframes all work as input.
  It also preserves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, and entities appear and disappear on the right frame.
  We implement AnyGameRenderer by LoRA fine-tuning MiniMax-H3 ref2va, a 33B reference-video-conditioned video generation model. Training uses sim10k paired clips from three sources: (i) multi-stream rendering data from 38 agent-made games exported from GEAR, an AI game-creation tool; (ii) two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine, with programmatically controlled crowds, count changes, and entity scales; and (iii) real gameplay recordings, with pairs reconstructed via 3D-box detection.
  To evaluate the entity correspondence, we propose an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, scored against ground-truth boxes. Compared with the base model, AnyGameRenderer better preserves entity correspondence: temporal match rises from 50.9\% to 62.9\%, missed count changes fall from 34.7\% to 21.3\%, and fewer entities are hallucinated or left unrendered.
evidence_items.title: AnyGameRenderer: Entity-Consistent Generative Rendering Across Games and an Entity-Level Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: LLM memory is widely used in long-term conversation understanding. Agentic memory systems often use mutation, structural organization, learned retrieval strategies, or other complex operations. Is this complexity always necessary? We study Raw-RAG, a naive RAG baseline using dense retrieval and reranking over raw history to supply evidence to a reader LLM. Across LoCoMo, LongMemEval, MEME, and MemoryAgentBench, Raw-RAG ranks first among the compared memory systems in six of seven benchmark-model settings, outperforming the strongest compared agentic memory system by 0.13-5.53 points. We investigate why raw-history retrieval remains competitive. Evidence analysis shows that its higher coverage of necessary evidence can offset lower utilization. Useful evidence includes both answer values and the relations and dependency paths needed to derive them. Even complete access to transformed memory stores leaves an accuracy gap relative to raw evidence, highlighting the importance of preserving raw information. These findings challenge the necessity of complex agentic memory for the evaluated conversation tasks and establish naive RAG as an essential baseline.
evidence_items.title: Is Complex Agentic Memory Always Needed? Naive RAG Is Stronger Than We Thought

evidence_items.summary: Deep research agents synthesize open-web evidence into long reports, but current benchmarks do not evaluate research centered on a source video. We introduce Video-Centered Deep Research Report Generation. Given a video and user request, an agent identifies research questions, retrieves external multimodal evidence, and produces an interactive report linked to relevant video moments. This task has direct practical value because it helps users locate relevant moments, verify claims, reproduce demonstrated procedures, and make informed decisions from video content. We present a skill-based workflow and OmniDR-Bench for this task. For evaluation, we propose Omni Atomic Rubric Trees (Omni-ARTs). Each tree contains three dimensions, 23 shared directions, and task-specific atomic binary criteria. The directions test audiovisual grounding, multimodal evidence use, and interactive presentation. Audited Rubric Construction (ARC) builds these trees through independent evidence collection, automated checks, behavioral calibration, and iterative human review. OmniDR-Bench contains 50 Chinese and English tasks across 19 realworld subcategories. It includes 6,414 criteria. Across 18 agent configurations, the best system scores 63.3 out of 100. Current agents still need broader content coverage, stronger causal and logical analysis across modalities, and more accurate citation support. We further analyze models, harnesses, skill configurations, video categories, and research trajectories. The code and data are released at https://github.com/marinero4972/OmniDR-Bench.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Watching and Searching: Benchmarking Agents for Video-centered Deep Research Reports

evidence_items.summary: Policy enforcement for LLM agents has shifted from single-turn content moderation to compound, application-specific policies evaluated over multi-turn transcripts and tool-call trajectories. Fine-tuned guardrail models are efficient but degrade on compound policies, and while LLM-as-a-judge approaches achieve higher accuracy, they incur high inference cost and tend to produce unstable predictions. Neurosymbolic methods offer a natural alternative, decomposing the policy into narrow neural decisions composed under explicit logic. However, existing symbolic layers lack the required expressiveness and are optimized against fixed data rather than the policy itself. To address this, we introduce SCOPE, which compiles a policy into an executable program of neural predicates executed by small models, deterministic extractors, and code that composes their outputs. The program is optimized jointly with its training data, using adversarial generation of counterexamples that target where the program deviates from the policy. We evaluate SCOPE on a benchmark of real-world policy tasks against prompt optimization, task decomposition, and workflow generation methods, achieving the highest average accuracy across tasks and models. Programs optimized with the weakest executor transfer to other models without further optimization. This allows them to be deployed in production on inexpensive models, where they reach accuracy comparable to frontier reasoning models. Unlike these monolithic models, SCOPE produces substantially more stable predictions, and each verdict is interpretable through the predicate outputs that produced it. Additionally, we validate the key components of our method through an ablation study. SCOPE thus enables reliable, interpretable, and efficient policy enforcement at production scale.
evidence_items.title: SCOPE: Compiling Natural-Language Policies into Neurosymbolic Predicate Programs

evidence_items.summary: Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.
evidence_items.title: Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video

evidence_items.summary: Despite substantial progress in Deep Search agents, their ability to conduct end-to-end research in real-world open Web environments remains insufficiently evaluated. Unlike static retrieval settings, information on the real-world Web is distributed across diverse sources, modalities, and heterogeneous formats, often involving complex interaction mechanisms that require agents to autonomously search for, access, and integrate relevant evidence during execution. To address this gap, we introduce the OpenDS task, designed to evaluate agents' ability to perform multi-step deep search in the live, open Web. This task requires agents to autonomously explore the real Web, discover and connect relevant evidence from multiple independent sources through Web search, browser interaction, and evidence processing, and ultimately determine a unique factual answer. Building on this task formulation, we construct OpenDS-World, a benchmark comprising 200 challenging tasks spanning diverse information modalities, heterogeneous file formats, and interactive access requirements, with independent human verification to ensure evidence validity and answer uniqueness. We evaluate 12 frontier models under a unified tool environment and execution protocol. The best-performing model achieves 39.0% accuracy, while human evaluation across 1,000 independent attempts yields 21.1% accuracy. Further analyses of tool usage, search cost, termination behavior, and failure recovery reveal substantial differences in research strategies across models, as well as persistent challenges in tool coordination and long-horizon search management. OpenDS-World provides a unified evaluation platform for systematically assessing and advancing agents' autonomous deep search capabilities in real-world open Web environments.
evidence_items.title: Deep Search in Real-World Web Environments

evidence_items.summary: High-quality image editing requires precise modification of target regions while preserving the content of unrelated regions. Existing editing models produce flattened outputs that limit precise local manipulation and layer reuse, while decomposition methods typically optimize layer recovery separately from instruction-driven editing. To this end, we introduce LayerEditor, a unified framework that couples instruction-guided image editing with controllable generation of reusable RGBA layers. At its core, In-Context RGB-Alpha Token Modeling jointly represents the edited canvas and an ordered sequence of RGB-Alpha layers within a single token sequence, enabling semantic edits and explicit control over individual layer content. To retain the pretrained model's editing capability during adaptation to layered outputs, we propose Compositional Edit-Prior Distillation, which transfers its editing prior to both the edited canvas and the image composed from the predicted layers. To support training and evaluation, we construct LayerEditor-100K, a large-scale paired image-editing dataset with ordered RGBA layer annotations, and introduce dedicated benchmarks for layered editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LayerEditor maintains strong editing fidelity while generating accurate RGBA layers, supporting both flexible layer-level manipulation and multi-layer decomposition.
evidence_items.title: Editing Images into Reusable Layers via Compositional Edit-Prior Distillation

evidence_items.summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) relies on evaluation feedback to assess progress and guide further research, yet repeatedly running complex benchmarks is costly and slows iteration. Human experts reduce this cost by selecting benchmark subsets or designing compact suites. We ask whether AI agents can automate this design process and introduce EvalResearchBench (ERB), a benchmark for autonomous evaluation research. Given target materials, development references, candidate APIs, and fixed time and API budgets, an agent called the researcher selects or synthesizes tasks, implements graders, and revises them in pilot tests before freezing an executable evaluator for coding, co-work, and reasoning. We study 9 researchers and 13 candidate models and compare each frozen evaluator with 14 target benchmarks on score concordance and pairwise agreement. The best evaluators order about 75\% of candidate pairs as the targets do, below the 91\% ceiling set by disagreements among the targets. No researcher leads on every metric, and the best evaluator on development targets is not the best on sealed targets hidden from the researcher. A human-designed sample of public tasks remains a strong baseline, and the evaluator with the lowest recorded execution cost attains the highest pairwise agreement. Agents repair tasks and graders through pilot feedback, yet their evaluators can still truncate answers, exhaust the evaluation budget, or let a few questions dominate a domain score.
evidence_items.title: EvalResearchBench: Can AI Agents Build Their Own Feedback for Recursive Self-Improvement?

evidence_items.summary: Event sequences are chains of random events, each described by heterogeneous (numerical and categorical) features. The problem of event sequence forecasting occurs in finance, healthcare, business process intelligence, and other fields. In this work, we study multi-horizon forecasting of event sequences as a conditional generative modeling problem. We evaluate forecasts not only for prediction accuracy, but also for distributional realism. To this end, we present a benchmark comprising metrics for both quality aspects, strong statistical baselines, recent models adapted from adjacent fields, and curated real-world datasets. Careful evaluation reveals that no method excels at both accuracy and realism, highlighting a fundamental trade-off between the two. Finally, we introduce Wasserstein BaryBooster, an algorithm that aggregates samples from a realism-strong diffusion model into a state-of-the-art predictor, demonstrating that distributional realism can be converted into prediction accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/xaosina/event-sequence-forecasting.
evidence_items.title: Realism VS Accuracy: Event Sequence Forecasting from a Generative Modeling Perspective

evidence_items.summary: Navil-120 is a bilingual social-pragmatic dialogue training corpus engineered for autistic children in colloquial Chennai Tanglish (code-mixed Tamil and English in Roman script) and Tamil script. The dataset draws pedagogical foundations from Carol Gray’s Social Stories™ and evidence-based social skills intervention literature. It consists of 120 curriculum lessons spanning 140 conversation turns across four social interlocutors: - Father (Chores, meal status reporting, polite interruption, transitions) - Teacher (Classroom decorum, formal honorifics, seeking permission) - Friend (Playground negotiation, turn-taking, sharing, sportsmanship) - Stranger (Differentiating community courtesy from critical safety refusals) The curriculum is partitioned into: 1. Tier 1: 100 single-turn foundational lessons 2. Tier 2: 20 multi-turn interactive milestone scenarios Each lesson turn is explicitly annotated with expected communicative intents, acceptable alternatives, social/safety violations, required pragmatic features, model answers, and state transitions.
evidence_items.title: Navil-120: A Curated Code-Mixed Tamil-English (Tanglish) Social-Pragmatic Communication Dataset for Autism

evidence_items.summary: Logical reasoning is a highly valued capability in language models. However, high-quality logical reasoning data remain scarce, while manual data creation is costly and time-consuming. We introduce Operations Research Aided Synthesis (ORAS), a solver-verified, two-layer incremental framework for synthesizing logic question-answering data. ORAS leverages operations research techniques to systematically generate high-quality datasets for evaluating large language models (LLMs) and, when used for training, improving their reasoning capabilities. ORAS's pipeline integrates mathematical programming methods to generate question-answer pairs, and then employs a dual-phase approach: the first phase uses optimization algorithms to construct and evaluate the logic systems by solving the problem using a mathematical solver. The second phase translates the logic system to human-readable problems and generates answers according to the information from the mathematical solver. The fine-tuned model achieves a 22%-33% (percentage point) improvement in accuracy on in-sample tests and a 4%-22% (percentage point) improvement on similar out-of-sample tests.
evidence_items.title: Synthesis of Reliable Logic Question Answering Data for Large Language Model with Aid of Operations Research Program

evidence_items.summary: Aim: Global Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with cultural nuances. This pilot study investigates the feasibility of “Kumru,” a developing native Turkish LLM, in interpreting culturally specific emergency triage vignettes compared to standard medical terminology.Materials and Methods: A prospective in-silico study was conducted using a pilot dataset of 50 clinical vignettes based on Turkish Ministry of Health (Annex-4) Guidelines. The dataset was stratified into standard medical terminology (n=31) and cultural idioms (n=19) to assess domain-specific linguistic processing.Results: The model achieved 93.7% sensitivity for high-acuity cases but exhibited a specificity of 0% and an over-triage rate of 52%. While overall diagnostic accuracy was moderate (44.0%), the model demonstrated statistically superior performance in decoding cultural idioms (84.2%) compared to standard terminology (19.3%, p &lt; .001).Conclusions: Although the current native model demonstrates a high capability for understanding local idioms, its low specificity renders it operationally inefficient for autonomous clinical decision-making. These findings present a proof-of-concept for linguistic localization but highlight the necessity for extensive fine-tuning before clinical deployment.
evidence_items.title: Preliminary evaluation of a native Turkish large language model in emergency triage: a pilot study on cultural vs. standard terminology

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background The increasing availability of machine-readable research data has created a growing need for efficient large-scale data harmonization (DH). Although large language models (LLMs) show promise for reducing the time and labor required for DH, their effective integration into harmonization workflows remains an important methodological challenge. Objective This study aims to develop and evaluate a semiautomated, human-in-the-loop (HITL) LLM-assisted DH workflow as a proof of concept across 8 projects within a research consortium focused on disparities in multiple chronic conditions. Methods We developed an LLM-assisted DH workflow that combined preprocessing, semantic mapping, variable response mapping, synthetic data generation, data transformation, and iterative researcher review. Using Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT-4o) hosted in a secure academic environment, project-specific survey items were mapped to 114 Consortium Common Data Element (CDE) semantic groups. Semantic mapping accuracy was evaluated based on the Consortium’s consensus harmonization results. Complete and incomplete semantic mappings were distinguished according to construct overlap, and incomplete mappings requiring context-dependent human judgment were excluded for mapped item pairs and CDE semantic groups with and without HITL review. Results Following preprocessing, 884 survey items were included in the DH workflow, of which 812 were mapped to a mean of 79 CDE semantic groups per project. Mean semantic mapping accuracy for item pairs was 95.9% (SD 5.7%) with HITL review and 86.7% (SD 8.6%) without HITL review. At the CDE semantic-group level, the corresponding accuracies were 98.9% (SD 1.7%) and 94.9% (SD 4.0%), respectively. Across projects, omission of valid semantic mappings occurred more frequently than incorrect semantic mappings, particularly for heterogeneous response structures and subjective constructs measured using different instruments.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model–Assisted Semiautomated Data Harmonization Pipeline for the Multiple Chronic Disease Disparities Research Consortium: Framework Development and Comparative Validation Study

evidence_items.summary: Although social media has become a central arena for deliberative discourse, debates are frequently characterized by incivility. Due to the volume of online discourse, it is challenging to assess when and where interventions, such as community-based counterspeech, are required. Accordingly, automated measurement of deliberative quality is a powerful tool for facilitating constructive online communication. Since deliberation is multidimensional, attempts to monitor online discourse must consider alternative forms of communication to foster inclusive deliberation. Whereas Type I deliberative dimensions, such as rationality and civility, are grounded in Habermasian ideals, Type II deliberation extends this perspective by incorporating alternative communicative forms, including emotionality and storytelling, into a more inclusive assessment of deliberative quality. Addressing the limitations of prior studies that primarily focused on classic Type I deliberative dimensions and tested only a small number of large language models, this study evaluates multiple open-weight models to conduct a nuanced assessment of deliberative quality. We applied the large language model that achieved the best overall balance between predictive performance, model size, and computational efficiency to a dataset of 64,223 comments from German-language climate change discourse on X. Our results demonstrate that large language models can reliably capture complex Type II deliberative dimensions despite class imbalances and subtle linguistic cues that generally hinder automated text classification. Class imbalance often impairs classification performance due to highly skewed label distributions, and Type II dimensions are particularly difficult to detect as they are often signaled by implicit, context-dependent markers.
evidence_items.title: Can AI Gauge Deliberative Quality? Evaluating Deliberation on Social Media With Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: The increasing volume and complexity of environmental data have highlighted the need for advanced analytical and artificial intelligence methods to support water-resource monitoring and management. Although machine-learning (ML) models have achieved strong performance in water-quality prediction and classification, their black-box nature remains a major obstacle to their use in environmental decision-making and policymaking. This study presents an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-based framework for two complementary water-quality assessment tasks: three-class water quality index classification using Dataset A and binary water-potability classification using Dataset B. Eight machine-learning algorithms were evaluated: logistic regression, support vector machine, random forest, extremely randomized trees, bagging classifier, multilayer perceptron, light gradient boosting machine, and categorical boosting. Five-fold stratified cross-validation was used to improve the reliability and generalizability of the evaluation. Shapley additive explanation, local interpretable model-agnostic explanations, permutation importance, and partial dependence plots were applied to interpret model behavior and extract domain-relevant insights. LightGBM achieved the highest mean accuracy for the minimum-value subset of Dataset A (0.946 ± 0.010), whereas CatBoost achieved the highest mean accuracy for the maximum-value subset (0.956 ± 0.006). For Dataset B, Extra Trees achieved the highest mean accuracy (0.682 ± 0.015). The interpretability analyses identified pH, dissolved oxygen, biochemical oxygen demand, conductivity, and microbiological indicators as influential predictors within Dataset A, whereas pH, total dissolved solids, turbidity, and other physicochemical variables contributed prominently to the binary potability predictions in Dataset B.
evidence_items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence-Based Framework for Water Quality Index Classification: A Multi-Dataset Comparative Analysis Using Machine Learning and Model Interpretability

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Machine learning has moved from proof of concept to routine operation in pharmaceutical quality control, yet the autonomy it is granted narrows sharply as products approach release. In this narrative review, we propose that this unevenness reflects not model capability but the regulatory burden an output must clear before it can be acted on, a pattern we term the validation‐barrier gradient. We score this barrier across four stages on criteria covering decision criticality under good manufacturing practice, validation and data‐integrity load, locus of legal liability, and patient‐safety consequence. The composite barrier rises as observed autonomy falls. At final product inspection, deep vision systems already detect defects at line speed, often on small single‐site datasets, but the authority to release a batch still rests with a qualified person. This gap between what a model can do and what it is allowed to decide cannot be explained by task difficulty alone. Closing it requires not further accuracy gains but shared benchmarks, routine robustness reporting, and change‐control pathways allowing validated models to be updated rather than frozen.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in pharmaceutical drug product quality control and assurance

evidence_items.summary: The excess energy and pressure of a strongly screened Yukawa fluid (screening parameter κ in the range of 5 ≤ κ ≤ 12) are calculated using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. These results are used to verify the accuracy of the variational approach that uses a fluid of hard spheres as a reference system, and the relatively high precision of this method is documented. We also show that the energy and pressure cannot be described by the ion-sphere model, which works well under weak screening. The Rosenfeld–Tarazona scaling for the thermal component of excess energy remains applicable, but in a slightly modified form compared with that in the weak-screening regime. The effective inverse-power-law exponent is determined. The excess entropy is evaluated using the variational approach and the MD excess energy data, and a good agreement is demonstrated. These results can be of some interest in the context of complex plasmas and colloidal suspensions as well as for systems in the vicinity of the soft-to-hard interaction crossover in general.
evidence_items.title: Strongly screened Yukawa fluids: Benchmark thermodynamics and the soft-to-hard interaction crossover

evidence_items.summary: Space-based missions such as CoRoT, , and TESS have revolutionised asteroseismology and strengthened its synergies with exoplanet science. With PLATO and ARIEL on the horizon, these synergies will play an even more central role. Kepler We revisit the characterisation of the nearby K dwarf HD 219134 using advanced seismic diagnostics. Our goals are to investigate the reported tension between asteroseismic and interferometric radii, update the fundamental parameters of the star, refine the properties of its planetary system, and investigate the coupled rotational, magnetic, and star–planet evolution of the system, including the atmospheric mass‑loss histories of its planets. The stellar characterisation is based on detailed asteroseismic forward modelling complemented by seismic inversions to quantify systematic uncertainties associated with non‑seismic constraints, assess the compatibility of radius measurements, and evaluate the impact of surface modelling on seismic inferences. The revised stellar properties were used as inputs for rotational evolution investigations, stellar wind modelling, and high‑energy irradiation histories. Seismic inversions rule out the most recent interferometric radius determination, whereas asteroseismic and spectroscopic results are compatible with the previous interferometric measurement from 2019. We derive revised stellar mass, radius, and age of 0.779 ± 0.015 ± 0.006 , M ⊙, 0.753 ± 0.005 ± 0.002 , R ⊙, and 8.92 ± 0.89 ± 0.19 Gyr, respectively. The quoted systematic uncertainties reflect contributions from the non-seismic observational constraints only. Literature values for combined uncertainties arising from physical inputs and surface-effect prescriptions are 0.007M ⊙, 0.002R ⊙, and 0.81 Gyr, respectively.
evidence_items.title: Detailed study of HD 219134: A benchmark K dwarf with a compact planetary system

evidence_items.summary: Active learning promises to reduce annotation cost by letting a model choose which unlabelled examples should be labelled next, but published gains vary widely and some strategies have been reported to perform worse than random selection. This study compares six query strategies under identical conditions on three real image datasets: handwritten digits from MNIST, product photographs from Fashion-MNIST and the smaller UCI Digits collection. Starting from 20 randomly chosen labelled images, a logistic-regression classifier was retrained after each batch of queries until 1,000 images (400 for Digits) had been labelled, with five random seeds per condition. The strategies were random sampling, least-confidence, margin and entropy uncertainty sampling, k-center greedy diversity sampling, and margin sampling combined with k-means diversification of each batch. Margin sampling with batch diversification was the most label-efficient strategy on all three datasets: it reached 95% of the accuracy of a model trained on the full pool with 372, 452 and 82 labels on average, whereas random sampling needed 750 and 216 labels on MNIST and Digits and reached the target in only one of five runs on Fashion-MNIST (at 820 labels), and its area under the learning curve exceeded that of random sampling in all 15 runs. However, least-confidence and entropy sampling were worse than random sampling throughout the budget on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, and k-center greedy sampling ended 16.3 and 9.9 percentage points below random sampling on these datasets. Inspection of the images queried by each strategy explained these failures: entropy sampling repeatedly selected visually similar ambiguous digits from a few classes, whereas k-center greedy selected atypical images, whose distance to their tenth-nearest neighbour was 1.38 and 1.82 times the pool median, and over-sampled particular classes. On the small Digits dataset all strategies outperformed random sampling.
evidence_items.title: When uncertainty sampling backfires: A benchmark of active learning query strategies on real image datasets

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Machine-learned force fields (MLFFs) based on Neuroevolution Potential (NEP) models were developed for the ionic liquid 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium acetate ([Emim][Ac]) using first-principles reference data generated with four density functionals: PBE-D3, RPBE-D3, optB88-vdW, and SCAN+rVV10. Using a unified training protocol, the resulting NEP models were systematically benchmarked against structural, thermophysical, transport, and hydrogen-bond-network properties, including radial distribution functions (RDFs), coordination numbers, neutron total scattering profiles, density, viscosity, ionic conductivity, and thermal conductivity. Spearman correlation analysis and weighted composite scoring were further used to establish a property-oriented evaluation framework for MLFF assessment and selection. The results reveal a pronounced dependence of NEP performance on the density functional used to generate the reference data. Although all four models reproduce the dominant local structural features of [Emim][Ac], appreciable differences emerge in medium-range structural ordering and transport properties. The PBE-D3-based NEP provides the most accurate overall description of structural properties, whereas the optB88-vdW-based NEP yields the closest agreement with experimental transport properties, particularly viscosity and ionic conductivity. Analysis of the hydrogen-bond network further reveals systematic relationships among hydrogen-bond populations, residence times, free-ion fractions, and ion transport. These results demonstrate that, for [Emim][Ac], the exchange–correlation functional used for reference-data generation influences the physical fidelity and property-specific performance of the resulting NEP models.
evidence_items.title:
Performance of
Neuroevolution Potentials for the Ionic
Liquid [Emim][Ac]: A Systematic Benchmark of Four Density Functionals

evidence_items.summary: Design errors carried over into construction lead to rework, material waste, and avoidable embodied carbon. Rule-based compliance checking in Building Information Modelling (BIM) can identify explicit design issues. However, current rule-based engines struggle to capture complex spatial arrangements and contextual geometric relationships among surrounding components. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a promising alternative by learning tacit, geometry-dependent conventions of expert practice directly from BIM data. Yet existing AI approaches either learn from 2D representations or rely on handcrafted geometric features that presuppose the target rules. We conduct a controlled study on a parametric benchmark derived from a single apartment plan. A graph transformer predicts where a masked door belongs along a known host wall. It learns from BIM topology and pose-conditioned neural signed distance function (SDF) embeddings, without explicit coordinate features. On unseen rigid transforms, the model achieves 79.1% side accuracy. A graph attention baseline reaches 68.9%, and a message-passing baseline stays at chance. On a second plan with a different topology, it reaches 68.2%. Doubling the training data does not raise this. Without retraining, the first plan’s model reaches 74.0% on the second. Performance on an unseen room-semantic configuration falls to chance. This is a necessary step towards learning tacit design conventions.
evidence_items.title: Recovering Predefined Door-Placement Rules from BIM Geometry: A Controlled Benchmark of Graph Transformers over Neural Signed Distance Function Embeddings

evidence_items.summary: Hospital patient services (registration and appointment scheduling) often face fragmented systems, long handling times, and data-entry errors, while patients expect instant 24/7 digital interactions. This study uses Design Science Research to develop a prescriptive five-phase framework for CRM-integrated agentic AI, whose novelty lies in combining bounded transactional agency, middleware-mediated access to CRM/SIMRS tools, and staged governance. Its design assumptions are evaluated through a controlled proof of concept (PoC). The PoC implements an end-to-end transactional conversational workflow (WhatsApp/web chat) in which an LLM-based agent uses API middleware to call tools on a CRM/SIMRS sandbox, avoiding direct database access. The artefact structures are: preparation and alignment; analysis and detailed design; implementation and controlled testing; pilot and evaluation; and scaling and institutionalization, supported by governance mechanisms (clinical “green/red” boundaries, audit logging, and human-in-the-loop supervision). Empirical evaluation applied black-box testing across 15 positive and negative scenarios comprising 285 executions. Of these, 246 met the predefined scenario criteria, and 39 failed, yielding an overall controlled-scenario success rate of 86.32%. A separate message-level latency log contained 292 message-response pairs across 58 recorded conversation groups; median response time was 9 s (IQR 4–19 s), with 88.70% of responses returned in under 30 s and 97.26% in under 60 s. Selected persisted CRM records were additionally checked through authorized visual inspection, with no discrepancies observed. These findings support technical feasibility under controlled PoC conditions while identifying patient-centred evaluation, cybersecurity assessment, production load testing, economic evaluation, longitudinal monitoring, and multi-site validation as requirements for broader deployment.
evidence_items.title: A Prescriptive Design Framework for CRM-Integrated Agentic AI in Hospital Patient Services: Design Science Development and Empirical Proof-of-Concept Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The increasing digitalization of smart grids exposes cyber-physical infrastructures to sophisticated false-data injection, communication spoofing, and supply-chain attacks, challenging the reliability of conventional intrusion detection under previously unseen operational conditions. Although machine-learning models can identify anomalous patterns, predictive discrimination alone does not establish whether automated decisions are safe, explainable, or operationally accountable. This study introduces GRIDGUARD-AI, an explainable, safety-assured agentic investigation framework integrating random forests (RF), temporal convolutional networks (TCN), and autoencoder (AE)-based anomaly detection with deterministic risk escalation, evidence-grounded AI investigations, and human-in-the-loop (HITL) governance. Using the Data4Cyber dataset, eight-fold leave-one-scenario-out evaluation examines 14,202 rolling windows containing 141 variables across eight operational scenarios. Results reveal substantial cross-scenario variability in detector discrimination, reinforcing the importance of evaluating generalization beyond familiar attack conditions. An exploratory three-way assurance policy classified 1,697 windows as SAFE, 501 as AUTO ALERT, and 12,004 as HUMAN REVIEW. Of 8,455 attack windows, 138 were incorrectly released SAFE (1.63%), yielding 98.37% attack escalation into automatic alert or human review rather than equivalent detection accuracy. Sequential AI-agent investigations completed 24/24 cases after quota-related retries, while automatic tool-calling workflows completed 8/8 scenario probes. Despite demonstrating traceable evidence handling and bounded investigation capabilities, the substantial human-review burden (84.52%), concentrated false-safe failures, and post-hoc policy refinement prevent claims of deployment-ready protection.
evidence_items.title: GRIDGUARD-AI: Scenario-Held-Out Cyberattack Detection with Explainable Assurance and Bounded Agentic Investigation

evidence_items.summary: Municipalities increasingly delegate healthcare, social assistance, utilities, transit, and identity verification to semi-autonomous systems. Real-world failures, including Australia's Robodebt scheme and the Dutch childcare benefits scandal, show that automated administration can strip life-sustaining services from large populations whose formal entitlements never changed. Existing governance responses remain fragmented across sectoral silos, with none enforcing a computationally verified constraint at the individual level across multiple domains concurrently. We present \HSC{}, a multi-agent framework that operationalizes essential human functioning as a non-compensatory constraint on automated municipal allocation. The architecture establishes a per-resident capability floor over ten normalized dimensions, identifying deprivation via an Alkire--Foster dual cutoff so that surplus in one domain cannot offset deficits in another. A Human Sovereignty Gate evaluates candidate allocations by measured worst-case capability impact and reversibility, recording commitments in an auditable ledger for which we prove that no admissible sequence of automated decisions can cross the floor. A Basic Needs Assurance Engine coordinates sector agents over a cyclic dependency graph to block cross-sector cascades, backed by an offline resilience reserve during platform outages. We derive a feasibility bound showing that individual risk tolerance cannot be legislated to zero, and specify an agent-based evaluation protocol for 250{,}000 synthetic residents across six disruption scenarios.
evidence_items.title: Human Sovereignty in the Agentic City: Enforcing Multi-Sector Capability Floors Against Automated Deprivation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial intelligence agents now search, evaluate, negotiate, and pay on behalf of consumers, while firms deploy agents that create content, personalize offers, and complete transactions. Agentic commerce therefore weakens a foundational assumption of marketing thought and marketing measurement: that the recipient of marketing activity is a human being. The evidence is scattered across marketing, information systems, computer science, economics, and law, and it has a largely forgotten first act in the shopbot research of the late 1990s. Following the SPAR-4-SLR protocol with PRISMA 2020 reporting, we screen 5,157 records from Scopus, Web of Science, and EBSCO Business Source and add verified snowballing to assemble 140 primary studies spanning 1994 to 2026. Each study is coded on influence direction, customer journey stage, delegation depth, method, and research wave. The synthesis yields an actor taxonomy with a five-level delegation ladder, an influence triad that separates marketing to, through, and by agents, an integrated account of trust and governance infrastructure, and a market-level analysis connecting both research waves. The Agentic Commerce Reference Framework consolidates this evidence into four auditable layers with explicit cross-layer dynamics, a ten-proposition research agenda, and five measurement instruments for analytics practice. A complete replication package accompanies the article.
evidence_items.title: When the customer is a machine: a systematic literature review and integrative framework of agentic commerce

evidence_items.summary: HEP-ZAV (from the Spanish Herramienta de Evaluación de Proyectos en Zonas de Alta Vulnerabilidad) is an Excel-based, AHP-weighted multi-criteria decision-support tool for the ex ante assessment of development projects in highly vulnerable territories. It transforms a territorial diagnosis into a structured, weighted and traceable evaluation matrix of three levels, eleven factors, fifty-six sub-factors and one hundred and sixty-eight indicators, and reports a three-component suitability profile (implementing-team capacity, project-territory compatibility and contextual feasibility) rather than a single composite score. All indicators share a common suitability direction, so adverse conditions are scored as project adaptation or mitigation and no score inversion is required. The official weights come from a group Analytic Hierarchy Process (consistency ratio <= 0.10, group consensus > 70%). This record contains the tool (a blank template and a worked education-centre example), the user manual (Word and PDF) and the Python code for the Monte Carlo and sensitivity analyses. The tool is diagnostic and transferable; it is not a validated predictor of project success.   How to cite: If you use HEP-ZAV in your work, please cite the software: Desravines, R.; Petrus-Bey, J.M.; Ruiz-Pérez, M. (2026). HEP-ZAV: Ex Ante Project Evaluation Tool for Highly Vulnerable Territories (Version 1.2) [Software]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23612995 Please also cite the associated article (when available): Desravines, R.; Petrus-Bey, J.M.; Ruiz-Pérez, M. A Multi-Criteria Framework for the Ex Ante Evaluation of Development Projects in Highly Vulnerable Territories: Methodological Design from Canaan (Haiti).

evidence_items.summary: The pendok, a metal covering for a keris's wooden sheath, serves both protective and artistic functions. Preliminary observations at keris markets, tosan aji communities, and pendok workshops in Surakarta and Imogiri indicated that multiple batik motifs are rarely used within a single pendok composition. This study aims to develop a Surakarta-style bunton pendok design that combines parang, Sulur Alas-alasan, and Truntum motifs. Using a qualitative, practice-based research approach, the study involved observation, literature review, interviews, visual exploration, design development, and aesthetic evaluation. The three motifs, Sulur, Alas-alasan, and Truntum, signify life and growth, while Truntum conveys guidance, fidelity, and hope. The resulting design arranges the motifs across the upper, middle, and lower sections of the Surakarta-style bunton pendok. The study offers a design approach for adapting batik motifs to keris metalwork and contributes to the development of tradisional craft ornament.
evidence_items.title: Designing A Surakarta-Style Bunton Pendok Through the Composition of Parang, Sulur Alas-Alasan, And Truntum Batik Motifs

evidence_items.summary: In Bangladesh, for instance, climate change is a core socio-economic and environmental issue that has lifted thousands of people in their gender-specific exposure along with the socio-economical and institutional barriers. The objective of this study was to evaluate analysis women climate change exposure, gendered vulnerability, adaptive capacity and its influence on climate adaptation practices and climate resilience with the goal of elucidating pathways long fostering resilience. A quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted using a survey of 384 women aged 18 years or above within climate-vulnerable communities in Bangladesh. The data were collected using a structured questionnaire based on five point Likert scale and analyzed the data using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlation and multiple regression techniques. Exposure to climate change was substantial, especially regarding the disruption of livelihoods and income (76%), food insecurity (87%), water insecurity (85%) and damage to household assets (79%). Gendered vulnerability was highly present as well, especially related to safe provision of shelter and sanitation, ownership of productive assets and access to financial resources and decision-making, as well as caregiving workload. The respondents displayed moderate to comparatively high adaptive capacity exhibiting various adaptation practices such as household preparedness, asset protection and livelihood adjustment, disaster preparedness. Adaptation to climate change was relatively strong; recovery of livelihood and income was, however, more difficult. Ultimately the results demonstrate that increasing women economic resources, decision-making participation, diversification of livelihoods, access to climate information and community-based disaster preparedness can improve long term resilience.
evidence_items.title: Climate Change and Gendered Vulnerability in Bangladesh: Mapping Women's Exposure, Adaptive Capacity, and Resilience Pathways

evidence_items.summary: As digital environments have moved to the center of daily life, the ways in which people present themselves and seek approval have undergone a profound transformation. This review addresses, from a clinical psychology perspective, the visibility of narcissistic personality traits in the digital age and their relationship with social media use. The study evaluates the conceptual framework and dimensions of narcissism, its distinction from healthy self-esteem, the debate over its cross-generational course, the reward and reinforcement processes of social media, the culture of likes and selfies, the clinical outcomes, and the approaches to intervention, in light of current meta-analyses and large scale studies. The evidence shows that there is a small to moderate and consistent association between grandiose narcissism and social networking behavior, and that quantified feedback can establish a cycle that reinforces approval seeking. It is emphasized that grandiose and vulnerable narcissism relate to social media in different ways and that cultural context moderates this relationship. The review proposes that narcissistic traits be evaluated within a nonstigmatizing, dimensional and developmental framework, and that integrated approaches targeting self-awareness, empathy, and the regulation of self-esteem be considered in intervention.
evidence_items.title: The Rise of Narcissistic Personality Traits in The Digital Age: an Evaluation of Social Media Use From A Clinical Psychology Perspective
