evidence_items.summary: A significant number of individuals from Generation Z have fallen victim to investment scams, with numerous reported cases resulting in substantial financial losses. This preliminary study analyzes structural factors rendering Gen Z vulnerable to online investment scams. Using a quantitative approach and structural equation modeling through Partial Least Squares (PLS-SEM) to evaluate the proposed research model. Data were collected systematically through an online survey in August 2026, and from the collected data, a filtering process was carried out, resulting in a final sample of 87 respondents. Structural path analysis revealed that four hypotheses were accepted, namely Financial Literacy to Investment Scam Awareness, Digital Literacy to Investment Scam Awareness, Financial Literacy to Victimization Propensity, and Perceived Trust to Investment Intention. However, the other four hypotheses were rejected, namely Financial Literacy to Investment Intention, Investment Intention to Victimization Propensity, Perceived Risk to Investment Intention, and Perceived Trust to Perceived Risk. These findings reveal a critical disconnect between the cognitive awareness and behavioral vulnerability of Generation Z. Although their understanding of financial literacy is increasing, this has paradoxically increased the likelihood of them becoming victims. Their investment choices are driven entirely by blind trust in platforms, rather than by objective risk assessment. This underscores the fact that conventional education is insufficient without psychological interventions and regulatory measures. This pilot mapping provides an empirical foundation for future anti-fraud strategies.
evidence_items.title: Mapping Gen Z Vulnerability to Investment Scam Through Digital Literacy and Financial Literacy in the Digital Information Environment

evidence_items.summary: This dataset was prepared from a cross-sectional online survey of 566 Iraqi adults conducted between July and September 2026. The study examined generative artificial intelligence use for health information, awareness of limitations, trust, verification practices, and willingness to act on generated information. The de-identified release retains all 566 respondents and contains 40 variables. Awareness and willingness measures apply to all respondents; experience-based trust and practice measures apply to the 443 previous health-information users. Structural blanks for the remaining 123 respondents indicate inapplicability. Timestamps, source identifiers, residence, employment, the health-status indicator (chronic condition or regular medication; q7), and four long-response fields without verified questionnaire option lists were withheld. Age and education were grouped, row order was shuffled, and four background fields were suppressed for 70 respondents (280 cells). Retained closed-question responses and score distributions are unchanged. The minimum group size of five applies only to the selected background-plus-eligibility combination. There are 564 distinct retained-answer patterns, including 562 respondents with singleton patterns; anonymity is therefore not guaranteed against detailed outside information. The release supports descriptive and factor-analytic reanalysis of the retained items and scores. The exact reported covariate-adjusted regressions cannot be fully reproduced because q7 was withheld and 70 background blocks were suppressed. Exact supplementary prediction cross-validation hashing and splits cannot be reconstructed from the withheld original fields. The data dictionary documents the released variables and their coding.
evidence_items.title: Use, Trust, Verification, and Willingness to Act on Generative Artificial Intelligence Health Information Among Iraqi Adults: A Cross-Sectional Study

evidence_items.summary: The integration of artificial intelligence and digital technologies into modern medicine has emerged as a significant advancement in contemporary healthcare. Rapid developments in computational methods, intelligent systems, and digital platforms are transforming medical diagnosis, treatment planning, disease prevention, patient monitoring, and healthcare administration. These innovations are creating new possibilities for improving clinical accuracy, supporting evidence-based decisions, and enhancing the efficiency and quality of healthcare services. The book Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation in Modern Medicine explores the growing influence of intelligent technologies and digital solutions across various areas of medical science. It highlights the applications of machine learning, deep learning, medical image analysis, predictive analytics, robotic-assisted procedures, telemedicine, and digital health records in contemporary clinical practice. These technologies have the potential to assist healthcare professionals in identifying disease patterns, evaluating clinical information, personalizing treatment strategies, and facilitating timely medical interventions. In addition to examining technological advancements, this book addresses the challenges associated with the implementation of artificial intelligence in healthcare. Important considerations include patient data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, ethical responsibility, regulatory compliance, and the reliability of AI-generated recommendations. The responsible integration of these technologies requires appropriate clinical validation, transparent decision-making, professional oversight, and continued attention to patient safety. Digital innovation must complement medical expertise rather than replace the essential judgment and compassion of healthcare professionals.
evidence_items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND DIGITAL INNOVATION IN MODERN MEDICINE

evidence_items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23613071 . 1. Summary of the Research and Overall Impression Context and main findings Non-pharmacological sleep modulation is an important clinical objective. Prior investigations using transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) during or prior to sleep have primarily applied fixed, uniform frequencies across cohorts. Building on their own preliminary ambulatory home data, this preprint evaluates pre-sleep, dual-frequency (theta + alpha) personalized tACS versus sham in 31 adults (mean age 56, range 30–70; mixed insomnia severity, 1 severe) using in-lab electrophysiological recordings across an unstated number of nights (presumably an acute single crossover night per condition). The authors report that active stimulation increased sleep efficiency (85.7% vs. 78.4%, p = 0.007; framed as a "13.4% improvement"), reduced sleep onset latency (6.7 vs. 14.7 min, p = 0.009), and increased total sleep duration (308.5 vs. 282.2 min, p = 0.008), concluding that personalized tACS is highly effective and holds promise for clinical interventions. Strengths and contribution The study addresses an important question with some solid methodological choices: A within-subject crossover design controlling for between-subject baseline variability; In-lab electrophysiological recording with manual AASM epoch staging by two scorers; A sham condition incorporating ramp-up and ramp-down phases; and Frequency personalization grounded in FOOOF spectral decomposition to isolate true oscillatory peaks from the 1/f aperiodic background. Overall impression and fundamental concerns While personalizing stimulation frequencies to an individual's endogenous brain rhythms is an innovative concept that deserves rigorous study, the manuscript rushes to claim dramatic efficacy through engineered metrics and selective reporting.
evidence_items.title: PREreview of "PERSONALIZED TRANSCRANIAL ELECTRICAL STIMULATION IMPROVES SLEEP – EARLY FINDINGS"

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents a comprehensive suite of Information Extraction systems developed for the GutBrainIE Task at the BioASQ Lab of CLEF 2026, aimed at elucidating the gut-brain interplay from biomedical literature. For the Named Entity Recognition (NER) subtask, we evaluate domain-specific BERT models, GLiNER architectures, and ensemble methods, incorporating distant supervision and data augmentation. Our GLiNER-based approach demonstrated superior robustness on unseen test data, securing second place. For Named Entity Recognition and Disambiguation (NERD), which we address as an entity linking problem, we propose a two-stage hybrid system—which also ranked second. It combines deterministic frequency-based gazetteers for in-vocabulary terms and tackles out-of-vocabulary disambiguation with PubMedBERT and a fine-tuned SapBERT embedding models. Finally, for Mention-level (M-RE) and Concept-level (C-RE) Relation Extraction, we contrast an encoder-based ATLOP architecture, supervised fine-tuning of an open-weights LLM (Qwen3.5-4B), and few-shot prompting of proprietary GPT-5 models (GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.5). Our Concept-level Relation Extraction system also ranked second in the respective subtask.
evidence_items.title: Do You Need a Frontier LLM, or Can Domain-Specific Encoders Compete in Gut–Brain Information Extraction?

evidence_items.summary: The development of modular artificial general intelligence (AGI) requires not only an architecture capable of coordinating specialized cognitive functions, but also a training-data strategy adapted to those functions. The composition, structure, provenance, and quality of training data influence the knowledge available to a model, the patterns it learns, and the capabilities it can develop. Treating the training corpus as a uniform collection of text therefore overlooks an important architectural question: what kinds of data are appropriate for different cognitive modules, and how should they be selected? This paper proposes a differentiated approach to training-data architecture for modular AGI. It considers two related challenges: the potential value of professional artifacts as structured material for specialized training, and the risks associated with sensitive technical content and the increasing presence of AI-generated material in publicly available text. Professional artifacts - including UX reports, product requirements documents, financial memoranda, technical specifications, incident analyses and the synopses that writers submit to publishers - already possess established structures shaped by professional practice. Their organization, terminology, and domain-specific content can provide a practical scaffold for segmenting and organizing training material. Rather than treating all source material as undifferentiated text, the proposed approach recommends considering professional documents as structured resources for developing specialized modules. At the same time, the information density that makes such artifacts useful may require particular care when they contain cybersecurity procedures, vulnerability descriptions, or other operationally sensitive information. A second challenge concerns the provenance and diversity of training data.
evidence_items.title: Training Data Architecture for Modular AGI: Corpus Quality, Specialization, and the Problem of Synthetic Contamination

evidence_items.summary: Efficient regeneration remains a central barrier to applying molecular improvement and gene edtiting in tropical forage grasses. In Rhodes grass (Chloris gayana Kunth), we adapted a published mesocotyl-based regeneration protocol reported for cultivar Tolgar and tested it across several breeding and commercial lines. While proliferative callus was readily induced, shoot recovery was not robust or reproducible in our material. Most cultures developed green bud-like structures followed by root-like growth. This response highlights a key biological challenge for increasing shoot regeneration competence. Here, we use Rhode grass as a system to test how explant developmental identity and hormonal environment influence the transition from callus proliferation to shoot recovery. Current experiments compare three strategically selected explant sources: mesocotyl tissue as a benchmark for published regeneration systems, shoot apical meristem explants including shoot tips and leaf whorls as candidates for future leaf/shoot based transformation, and root explants as an entry point for root-based transformation workflows. Treatments assess reduced levels of the synthetic auxin 2,4-D, low cytokinin supplementation during callus induction, and copper sulphate as a stress treatment. Cultures are maintained in darkness at 28 o C, subcultured every 2 weeks, and scored for callus induction, putative embryogenic callus frequency and morphology. This design tests whether reducing auxin strength and selecting developmentally competent explants can shift cultures from root-biased proliferation toward shoot regenerative states. By linking explant biology with transformation practicality, this work advances understanding of regeneration bottlenecks in recalcitrant C4 grasses and provides a foundation for future transformation, gene editing and forage-quality target validation.
evidence_items.title: From callus to shoots: Unlocking regeneration competence in Rhodes grass

evidence_items.summary: Semantic answer caching reduces inference cost by reusing previous responses but may repeatedly serve incorrect answers. Prior research primarily addresses cache matching, verification, and freshness, whereas this study investigates an error-attribution problem: grouping multiple request surfaces under shared source keys can concentrate incorrect answer exposure without proportionally increasing the total number of errors. We evaluated 500 category-balanced MMLU-Pro questions, six instruction-and-format variants, and two instruction-tuned models using fixed multiple-choice predictions. On 400 TEST questions, pairwise answer disagreement was 27.12% for Qwen2.5-3B and 26.90% for Mistral-7B. At a DEV-selected threshold of 0.96, TEST same-question matching achieved 98.59% precision and 99.97% recall. Semantic caching avoided 91.69–92.31% of modeled inference-token cost. Under Zipf demand, mean maximum cumulative wrong reuse per source key rose from 146.8 to 783.2 for Qwen and from 153.3 to 820.1 for Mistral. These approximately fivefold increases partly reflect different cache-key granularities: at the underlying-question level, maxima were 726.0 versus 783.2 and 745.8 versus 820.1, respectively. Net additional wrong labels relative to fresh computation were only 22.1 and 37.55 per 4800 requests. Exposure-aware refresh did not consistently improve accuracy or control-concentrated errors. Reliable cache evaluation should jointly consider correctness, computational cost, error exposure, and aggregation level.
evidence_items.title: When Reuse Repeats Mistakes: Answer Stability and Error Concentration in Large Language Model Semantic Caching

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive molecular subtype of breast cancer that needs to be identified accurately from pathology reports to inform decision-making. Large language models (LLMs) have been reported to show great potential in the automatic extraction of important oncology information from unstructured medical text. Objective We aimed to create and test an LLM-based approach for automatic biomarker extraction and TNBC subtype classification based on breast cancer pathology reports using prompt-engineering techniques. Methods In total, 532 breast cancer pathology reports from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) were used. Our approach extracted structured oncology features, such as estrogen receptor status, progesterone receptor status, HER2 status, tumor size, tumor grade, and tumor histology, which were used to identify TNBC. We tested 4 frontier models: GPT-4o mini (released July 18, 2024), GPT-4.1 nano (released April 14, 2025), GPT-5 nano (released August 7, 2025), and Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite. Results The designed framework was able to extract relevant biomarkers and clinicopathological attributes from unstructured pathology reports and allowed for the automated identification of patients with TNBC. Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite showed superior performance in the extraction of clinicopathological attributes. For all models investigated, chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting was shown to outperform other strategies, such as zero-shot and few-shot prompting, for both biomarker extraction and TNBC classification. GPT-4o mini using CoT prompts reported the highest performance for TNBC classification. Conclusions Using prompt-engineering techniques based on LLMs proved to be an efficient method of translating unstructured breast cancer pathology reports into structured clinical information. Moreover, it can be used to accurately identify the TNBC subtype.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model Framework for Structured Biomarker Extraction and Triple-Negative Breast Cancer Identification From Pathology Reports: Development and Evaluation Study

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT The complexity of preparing Merdeka Curriculum teaching modules and prompting constraints in generative artificial intelligence systems provided the background for designing the AIDERA (Artificial Intelligence for Digital Education and Research Advancement) website. This study aimed to evaluate the validity and practicality of the AIDERA application as an AI-assisted tool for preparing Merdeka Curriculum teaching modules relevant to educators' needs. Employing a Research and Development approach framed within the ADDIE model, this development evaluated a zero-prompt interaction mechanism based on parametric forms. Evaluation involved three domain experts and 23 teachers from SMK IPIEMS Surabaya. Data were collected using 1–5 Likert scale questionnaires supplemented with open-ended qualitative feedback fields to gather in-depth suggestions for improvement. Descriptive percentage analysis revealed an expert validation score of 96.67% (highly valid) and user practicality reaching 82.87% (highly practical). Document preparation time efficiency received the highest rating (87.83%), whereas operational independence and usability recorded the lowest achievement (79.13%). Qualitative findings highlighted several technical issues and system refinement notes, including the need for integrative tutorials, optimization of mathematical notation representation, improved responsiveness during simultaneous access, and content template flexibility. Although AIDERA demonstrates strong potential as a supporting tool for module preparation, objective evaluation regarding its impact on learning effectiveness still requires broader further testing. evidence_items.summary: Abstract Rapid advances in cancer genetics and genomics, pathophysiology, diagnostics, and therapeutics have substantially increased the complexity of clinical oncology. Integrating large and diverse data streams into timely, patient‐specific decisions provides a compelling rationale for incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) into cancer care. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) encompasses several classes of models capable of generating new content. This clinically focused review concentrates on GenAI applications based primarily on large language models (LLMs) and vision‐language models (VLMs), as well as emerging agentic systems that use these models to perform coordinated, multistep tasks. LLMs demonstrate substantial medical knowledge, strong performance on oncology‐related assessments, and emerging capabilities in clinical reasoning. Guideline‐ and retrieval‐augmented systems can improve concordance with expert recommendations and interpretation of complex treatment algorithms. LLMs and VLMs have been applied to documentation, patient communication, information extraction and summarization, clinical decision support, and multimodal data synthesis. However, performance varies substantially across tasks and clinical domains, with important limitations including incomplete or outdated information, training‐data bias, automation bias, and confabulation. Agentic AI represents an emerging extension of these technologies in which LLMs or VLMs are incorporated into systems capable of multistep planning, external information retrieval, specialized tool use, and iterative evaluation and refinement. Early oncology applications include evidence synthesis, multimodal clinical decision support, radiology, pathology, surgery, and individualized treatment planning.
evidence_items.title: Generative artificial intelligence in medical oncology: A clinically focused narrative review of large language, vision‐language, and agentic artificial intelligence systems

evidence_items.summary: Objective: To investigate the ability of machine learning to predict the development of cardiovascular complications (heart failure and myocardial infarction) and renal complications (nephropathy and chronic kidney disease) among people with diabetes mellitus and thus detect those at risk earlier. Methodology: Data from the UCI "Diabetes 130-US Hospitals" dataset was used. The number of encounters included in the dataset is more than 100,000. ICD-9 diagnostic codes were utilized to define cardiac and renal complications. Prior to building models, the data was prepared, cleaned, and features were engineered. XGBoost, CatBoost, and Random Forest machine learning models were developed and validated. Also, SHAP and LIME analyses were performed to make the process more transparent. Results: The best-performing algorithm proved to be CatBoost, which obtained an AUC score of 0.94 in case of cardiac complications and 0.79 in case of renal outcomes. The other algorithms performed relatively well as well. The predictors identified with the help of SHAP and LIME analysis turned out to be consistent with some known clinical risk factors. Conclusion: The presented results show that there is a lot of potential in using machine learning techniques for predicting cardiovascular and renal complications among people with diabetes. Machine learning models could help in managing patients proactively and could serve as a tool for doctors' decision making.
evidence_items.title: redictive Modeling for Diabetic Complications Using Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into medical research and publishing represents a transformative shift, offering unprecedented opportunities to streamline workflow efficiency, enhance language clarity, and accelerate scientific dissemination. However, this rapid technological adoption introduces ethical, epistemological, and procedural challenges, including concerns over data fabrication, automated bias, intellectual property infringement, and the erosion of scholarly accountability. A structured analysis of practical applications highlights a clear demarcation between acceptable supplementary uses and strictly prohibited practices. AI tools are unacceptable as co-authors, as authorship demands moral, legal, and scholarly accountability that non-human entities cannot possess. Similarly, generating or modifying clinical images and media using AI remains unacceptable due to the risk of data distortion and misrepresentation. Within the editorial domain, AI systems must not replace peer reviewers or editorial decision-makers. Uploading confidential manuscript content into external AI platforms violates author confidentiality, while automated algorithms lack the contextual judgment and critical reasoning necessary for peer evaluation and final publication decisions. Conversely, AI tools are acceptable for planning the structure of a manuscript, language and grammar corrections, translation, quantitative or qualitative data analysis, and formatting, provided their use is transparently disclosed and critically evaluated by human researchers. Ultimately, the ethical deployment of AI in medical literature hinges on the principle that technology must serve as an auxiliary tool rather than a replacement for human cognition. Human authors, peer reviewers, and journal editors retain full responsibility and accountability for the accuracy, integrity, and scientific validity of published work.
evidence_items.title: Medical publishing in the era of artificial intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Peer review is important in maintaining the quality of scholarly publishing, but the process faces challenges such as shortage of reviewers, delays, inconsistent judgements, and overlooked errors. These challenges have increased the need to consider the appropriate use of artificial intelligence (AI) in peer review. Completely excluding AI or allowing it to function as an autonomous reviewer may not adequately address these problems. A Human–AI Augmented Review model is therefore proposed, in which AI supports clearly defined tasks under human supervision, while reviewers and editors retain responsibility for interpretation, ethical judgement, and editorial decisions. Peer review involves both routine technical checks and complex scholarly evaluation. AI can assist with repetitive and rule-based tasks such as manuscript screening, consistency checking, reviewer identification, and identification of reporting gaps. Human reviewers are still needed to assess methodology, scholarly contribution, and ethical issues. Effective use of AI requires a clear division of responsibilities, verification points within the review process, and governance measures to address bias, hallucinations, confidentiality, and excessive reliance on automation. Careful and limited use of AI can improve efficiency and reduce avoidable errors while maintaining accountability and trust in peer review.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence as an Assistant in Research Evaluation and Peer Review: A Critical Case for Augmentation Without Replacement

evidence_items.summary: Circadian rhythms represent a key biological dynamic across all kingdoms of life. These cell-autonomous rhythms generated by a gene-regulatory network regulate processes in a time-of-day-specific manner primarily via transcriptional rhythms in a significant fraction of genes. The controlled experiment paradigm can be used to study causal effects at the molecular level using transcriptomic RNA-seq data even in this dynamic scenario. Multiple tools for the analysis of such data, termed differential rhythmicity (DR) analysis, are available but guidance on method choice remains limited. Here, we present a systematic benchmarking study of 12 different methods from 5 packages using a synthetic model of RNA-seq count data that incorporates both empirically estimated mean-dispersion trends and concomitant differential expression changes. By linking method performance to experimental conditions and analytical goals, we provide practical and simple rules of thumb that will help biologists choose appropriate DR methods and extract reliable biological insight from time series RNA-seq data.
evidence_items.title: Different, same, or arrhythmic: an empirically informed benchmark of differential rhythmicity methods

evidence_items.summary: This paper investigates two-dimensional knapsack problems modeled as the Generalized Two-Dimensional Knapsack Problem (G2KP), a variant not previously studied in the literature. The importance of the G2KP lies in its crucial role in designing Branch-Price-and-Cut (BPC) algorithms for the classical Two-Dimensional Bin-Packing Problem. We propose a novel and effective exact solution framework that incorporates both nonnumerically exact and numerically exact algorithms tailored to G2KP. The framework also achieves state-of-the-art performance on the well-known Two-Dimensional Knapsack Problem (with and without item conflicts) and the Two-Dimensional Orthogonal Packing Problem, solving several previously unsolved instances and establishing new benchmark results. These findings highlight the framework’s potential to inspire algorithmic developments for pricing problems in related BPC methods and higher-dimensional packing problems. To support future research, we make the algorithm code, instance data, and detailed results publicly available. History: Accepted by Andrea Lodi, Area Editor for Design & Analysis of Algorithms–Discrete. Funding: This study was supported by the Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72271062, 72671084, and 52575565], Science and Technology Projects in Guangzhou [Grant 2024A04J01019], and the Province Natural Science Fund of Guangdong [Grants 2025A1515011297 and 2024A1515010246]. Supplemental Material: The software that supports the findings of this study is available within the paper and its Supplemental Information ( https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/suppl/10.1287/ijoc.2025.1423 ) as well as from the IJOC GitHub software repository ( https://github.com/INFORMSJoC/2025.1423 ). The complete IJOC Software and Data Repository is available at https://informsjoc.github.io/ .
evidence_items.title: Exact Algorithms for Two-Dimensional Knapsack Problems: A Unified Framework with New Benchmark Results

evidence_items.summary: Correlations between objectives are natural in real-world multi-objective optimisation problems. They fundamentally shape the objective landscape and influence the search behaviour of a multi-objective optimiser. Existing continuous multi-objective benchmarks rarely provide the mechanisms to define them explicitly. We present BEACON-M, a continuous many-objective benchmark generator that constructs smooth objectives via Gaussian Process Random Fourier Features and offers explicit user-defined correlations. These correlations can be embedded via two distinct structured correlation matrix formats: single-group and two-group structures. BEACON-M instances are reproducible by construction, and their correlation structures satisfy analytically derived validity constraints. Beyond the generator itself, we analyse and characterise the feasible correlation region and show how correlations reshape dominance structure and objective landscapes. We also provide concrete guidelines for practitioners and algorithm developers to use these problems. To demonstrate the benchmark's use, we run experiments with state-of-the-art multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (dominance, indicator and decomposition-based) with different numbers of decision variables and objectives. Performance depends on the interaction between problem dimensionality (both in the objective and decision spaces) and the correlation structure and strength; no single algorithm is best across all settings, and which method performs best changes systematically with these factors. These findings demonstrate that such problems can inform the development of new algorithms, both Bayesian and evolutionary, and the selection of existing ones when solving a real-world multi-objective optimisation problem.
evidence_items.title: BEACON-M: Continuous Many-Objective Benchmark Problems via Gaussian Process Random Fourier Features with Explicit, Adjustable Correlation

evidence_items.summary: Hallucination-detection systems are usually judged by a single headline metric, computed under a benchmark design that determines what that metric can show. This paper’s contribution is not a detection algorithm — structural coherence scoring is established — but a methodology for measuring exactly what a benchmark proves and what it does not, applied to the SAS Multimetric Tribunal: a seven-module, GPU-free structural classifier combining lexical, entity-mutation, curvature, and logical-inversion signals via a cascading multiplicative penalty (\(\kappa {D} = 0.56\), \(\kappa {R} = 0.15\)). On a stratified 1,800-pair benchmark (HaluEval-Dialogue, HaluEval-QA, TruthfulQA), the tribunal reaches F1 = 98.99% with zero false positives under an A\(\rightarrow\)A identical-text sanity check. We report this figure and then show, using a format-controlled negative (N1) on the same 1,800 IDs, that it measures format asymmetry between source and response rather than hallucination detection. The tribunal flags 1,569 of 1,800 verbatim correct answers presented alone (87.2%), and in HaluEval-QA scores the correct answer as more anomalous than the hallucinated response. Three further findings follow from the same audit. (i) A per-module analysis shows the tribunal’s seven-module core has no content-sensitive module (prior to the optional R3.1 guard): the one module designed to capture semantic divergence (cre isi) gives the same per-ID score whether the response is byte-identical or completely different. (ii) The 87.97-point advantage of multiplicative combination over weighted averaging reported in v4 is an artifact of threshold calibration; under per-scheme thresholds on format-matched negatives, both schemes converge to F1 \(\approx 0.69\) and the multiplicative scheme is worse by AUROC.
evidence_items.title: SAS Multimetric Tribunal: What a Hallucination Benchmark Measures, and What It Does Not A Format-Controlled Audit of Structural Classification

evidence_items.summary: TRUSTWORTHY AUTONOMOUS BIOLABORATORIES THROUGH MICROROBOTICS AND QUANTUM SENSING AT THE LIMIT Replayable Experiments x Permission Governance x External Metrology STARLI Research Institute XXIX - Flagship Research Monograph 20 Can an autonomous biolaboratory become scientifically useful without acquiring the authority to redefine its own permissions, validate its own evidence, or release untraceable measurements? This nonclinical research monograph investigates a bounded laboratory architecture connecting microrobotic sample handling, quantum-enabled and classical sensing, independent metrological reference chains, experiment replay, physical safe stopping, and human authority. Its central proposition is that reliable autonomy is a property of the entire evidence pathway rather than of any single robotic manipulator or AI model. A laboratory result is eligible for release only when sample identity and integrity, authorized execution, traceable references, justified uncertainty limits, and external acceptance are all demonstrated. An apparently successful action is not equivalent to a scientifically accepted sample. Digital replay does not replace physical replication, cryptographic event integrity does not guarantee sensor truth, and a quantum hardware label does not establish a practical sensing advantage. The research design is developed across 82 chapter-level inquiries with five independently paginated investigations per chapter, 30 connected mathematical research plates, 200 distinct Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The chapters address typed authority graphs, specimen provenance, sample exposure, closed-chip physics, covariance-aware sensing, AI planning within finite action spaces, common-cause fault injection, external interlocks, blinded classical benchmarks, evidence DAGs, cross-site replication, data retention, and responsible system retirement.
evidence_items.title: TRUSTWORTHY AUTONOMOUS BIOLABORATORIES THROUGH MICROROBOTICS AND QUANTUM SENSING AT THE LIMIT  Replayable Experiments x Permission Governance x External Metrology  STARLI Research Institute XXIX - Flagship Research Monograph 20  Can an autonomous biolaboratory become scientifically useful without acquiring the authority to redefine its own permissions, validate its own evidence, or release untraceable measurements?  This nonclinical research monograph investigates a bounded laboratory architecture connecting microrobotic sample handling, quantum-enabled and classical sensing, independent metrological reference chains, experiment replay, physical safe stopping, and human authority. Its central proposition is that reliable autonomy is a property of the entire evidence pathway rather than of any single robotic manipulator or AI model.  A laboratory result is eligible for release only when sample identity and integrity, authorized execution, traceable references, justified uncertainty limits, and external acceptance are all demonstrated. An apparently successful action is not equivalent to a scientifically accepted sample. Digital replay does not replace physical replication, cryptographic event integrity does not guarantee sensor truth, and a quantum hardware label does not establish a practical sensing advantage.  The research design is developed across 82 chapter-level inquiries with five independently paginated investigations per chapter, 30 connected mathematical research plates, 200 distinct Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The chapters address typed authority graphs, specimen provenance, sample exposure, closed-chip physics, covariance-aware sensing, AI planning within finite action spaces, common-cause fault injection, external interlocks, blinded classical benchmarks, evidence DAGs, cross-site replication, data retention, and responsible system retirement.  The proposed minimum experimental prototype uses a closed microfluidic chip with interchangeable handling modules, two independently referenced readout channels, simulated or inert-tracer specimens, a separate audit service, and a physically verifiable stop mechanism. Proposed tests include unauthorized-action challenges, hidden calibration drift, interrupted events, sample contamination, unannounced network partitions, and independent laboratory replay or rerun.  DOI-linked scientific references establish the relevant literature in automated laboratories, microrobotics, quantum sensing, uncertainty metrology, FAIR data stewardship, and computational reproducibility. They do not independently validate the integrated system proposed here.  SCIENTIFIC STATUS AND LIMITATIONS  This book is a hypothesis-forming nonclinical research architecture. It reports no completed microrobotic or quantum biosensing experiments, no demonstrated clinical performance, no universal quantum advantage, and no autonomous system capable of authorizing itself. Statistical models, formulas, and decision policies require experimental verification, specialized review, and appropriate boundary conditions. A failed external reference, unavailable provenance chain, or revoked permission requires abstention rather than inference by convenience.  STARLI RESEARCH PHILOSOPHY  A trustworthy laboratory must remain answerable to evidence outside itself. Autonomy becomes scientifically meaningful when an experiment can be stopped, questioned, reconstructed, and handed to future researchers who retain the right to refuse its original assumptions.

evidence_items.summary: AUTONOMOUS FAILURE DIAGNOSIS FOR MICROROBOTICS AND QUANTUM BIOSENSING AT THE LIMIT Fault Trees × Measurement Credibility × Verified Safe Stopping STARLI Research Institute XXIX — Flagship Research Monograph 18 When a microrobotic sampling platform reports a plausible result, how can researchers determine whether the measurement is trustworthy—and whether the system should have stopped before reporting it? This research monograph investigates the scientific, statistical, and engineering foundations of autonomous failure diagnosis in microrobotic sampling and quantum-enabled biosensing. Rather than treating alarm accuracy as sufficient evidence of reliability, the study examines the entire measurement pathway, from physical actuation and raw detector signals to calibration references, uncertainty estimation, downstream inference, physical interlocks, and independently verifiable release decisions. The 771-page research architecture contains 82 chapters, 410 independently paginated research investigations, 30 interconnected mathematical studies, 200 Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Its principal investigations address sensor drift, common-mode reference failure, unknown-fault recognition, multivariate residual monitoring, sequential change detection, actuator latency, optical heating, microfluidic contamination, fault propagation, adversarial experimental design, and verified emergency stopping. A central research proposition is that correlation-aware, multi-source monitoring may reduce the release of corrupted measurements under previously unseen fault conditions compared with conventional fixed-threshold monitoring. The proposed experimental framework emphasizes independent fault injection, blinded evaluation, strong classical measurement comparators, explicit uncertainty accounting, and reproducible nonclinical hardware-in-the-loop testing. Particular attention is given to distinguishing detectable anomalies from identifiable root causes.
evidence_items.title: AUTONOMOUS FAILURE DIAGNOSIS FOR MICROROBOTICS AND QUANTUM BIOSENSING AT THE LIMIT  Fault Trees × Measurement Credibility × Verified Safe Stopping  STARLI Research Institute XXIX — Flagship Research Monograph 18  When a microrobotic sampling platform reports a plausible result, how can researchers determine whether the measurement is trustworthy—and whether the system should have stopped before reporting it?  This research monograph investigates the scientific, statistical, and engineering foundations of autonomous failure diagnosis in microrobotic sampling and quantum-enabled biosensing.  Rather than treating alarm accuracy as sufficient evidence of reliability, the study examines the entire measurement pathway, from physical actuation and raw detector signals to calibration references, uncertainty estimation, downstream inference, physical interlocks, and independently verifiable release decisions.  The 771-page research architecture contains 82 chapters, 410 independently paginated research investigations, 30 interconnected mathematical studies, 200 Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos.  Its principal investigations address sensor drift, common-mode reference failure, unknown-fault recognition, multivariate residual monitoring, sequential change detection, actuator latency, optical heating, microfluidic contamination, fault propagation, adversarial experimental design, and verified emergency stopping.  A central research proposition is that correlation-aware, multi-source monitoring may reduce the release of corrupted measurements under previously unseen fault conditions compared with conventional fixed-threshold monitoring.  The proposed experimental framework emphasizes independent fault injection, blinded evaluation, strong classical measurement comparators, explicit uncertainty accounting, and reproducible nonclinical hardware-in-the-loop testing.  Particular attention is given to distinguishing detectable anomalies from identifiable root causes.  A system may recognize that an observation is unreliable without possessing sufficient evidence to determine whether the underlying problem originates from the robotic actuator, sensing hardware, calibration reference, biological specimen, or data-processing pipeline.  Under such conditions, scientifically responsible operation requires abstention, quarantine, and independently verified stopping rather than unjustified confidence.  The 200 Research Gates introduce falsifiable scientific questions with proposed experimental protocols, measurable outcomes, competing explanations, and explicit rejection conditions.  The 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos preserve provisional research architectures that future investigators may challenge, reconstruct, divide, or replace as stronger evidence becomes available.  DOI-linked scientific literature provides methodological foundations in measurement science, fault detection, microfluidics, microrobotics, quantum sensing, and autonomous laboratory engineering.  Scientific Scope and Limitations  This monograph presents a hypothesis-forming, nonclinical research framework rather than completed experimental findings.  It does not guarantee comprehensive detection of unknown faults, establish autonomous nanoscale clinical systems, prove universal quantum sensing superiority, or authorize medical decisions.  Its proposed methods require independent experimental validation, specialized scientific review, and clearly defined operating boundaries.  STARLI Research Philosophy  A trustworthy autonomous research system must preserve the ability to recognize when its own evidence is insufficient.  Scientific intelligence is not demonstrated solely by producing an answer.  It is also demonstrated by knowing when an answer should be withheld.  By preserving falsifiable questions, physical evidence, uncertainty, and opportunities for independent reconstruction, this monograph invites future human and AI researchers to develop more reliable scientific instruments beyond the assumptions of its original design.

evidence_items.summary: Split language models keep input text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server. Attacks can reconstruct text from these messages. Comparing privacy evaluations is difficult when attackers see different messages, know different model weights or use different datasets and recovery measures. We present LLM-Attacker, a framework that records these choices and lets researchers check, compare and extend an evaluation. Compatible attacks reuse recorded messages, and their predictions are saved for independent scoring. The scoring rule requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass. Reports also identify attacks that remain untested. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding gradients returned during training increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%. The 95% interval for the token gain lay above the two-percentage-point threshold fixed before testing. This experiment is shared with a companion study; here, it tests how the evaluation responds to a change in attacker access. Further studies measure how corpus choice and compression defences affect recovery, compare an adapted published attack with its reference implementation, and test the measurement code. The framework reports implementation checks separately from measured attack effectiveness. Each privacy claim should state the attacker, dataset and scoring rule, report its controls and identify untested attacks.
evidence_items.title: The LLM-Attacker: A Unified Red-Team Framework for Privacy Evaluation of Split and Distributed LLM Systems

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) introduce unique quantization challenges due to their iterative denoising process. In this work, we reveal that quantization sensitivity is both taskand time-dependent, with different downstream tasks exhibiting distinct precision requirements across denoising steps. We further show that these patterns can be predicted without groundtruth labels or task-specific evaluation metrics. Building on these findings, we introduce T 2Quant, a task and time-aware mixedprecision quantization framework that uses a label-free sensitivity signal to optimally allocate activation precision across denoising steps under a fixed bit-width budget. Extensive experiments across three DLMs and six benchmarks demonstrate that T 2Quant consistently improves the average accuracy of existing quantization methods, achieving gains of up to 6.7 percentage points under the same budget.
evidence_items.title: Different Tasks, Different Timesteps: Temporal Task-Aware Quantization for Diffusion Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Complex camera motion is central to visual storytelling, yet translating cinematographic intent into controllable, executable camera trajectories remains challenging. We introduce FilmFlow, an agentic framework that converts natural-language instructions or reference videos into explicit camera trajectories for dynamic 3D environments. To generate these trajectories, a Director agent constructs executable camera plans by composing high-level motions from concurrent atomic operations that jointly control translation, rotation, and framing. The Director is supported by three specialized agents: an Interpreter that extracts scene-grounded cinematographic intent, a Scout that selects initial viewpoints, and a Critic that evaluates rendered results and provides visual feedback for iterative plan refinement. We also introduce CinemaBench, comprising 150 Blender scenes from self-created and licensed sources, with five camera instructions per scene for 750 text-directed tasks and 60 reference videos associated with a subset of scenes. CinemaBench supports evaluation of both text-directed camera generation and video reference-directed camera generation. Across a diverse set of evaluated baselines, FilmFlow achieves the strongest benchmark performance and the highest user preference, demonstrating effective spatial reasoning, temporal coordination, and visual composition for executable 3D cinematography.
evidence_items.title: FilmFlow: Agentic System for 3D Virtual Film Cinematography

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in video generation have made synthetic videos increasingly realistic, placing greater demands on reliable AI-generated video detection. Existing artifact-based detectors typically identify generation artifacts as evidence for source prediction, yet they may either fail to recognize subtle artifacts or reach the correct source decision without faithfully identifying the evidence underlying it. In this work, we systematically investigate how to design and train effective artifact detectors and formulate artifact detection as a structured process comprising three complementary capabilities: Inspection Planning, which determines what should be examined; Evidence Verification, which verifies whether the inspected content exhibits genuine generation artifacts; and Evidence Aggregation, which integrates the verified evidence into the final source decision. Building on this formulation, we introduce Verus-Insight, trained with human-anchored full-process supervision and progressive capability training to strengthen both fine-grained artifact detection and video-level detection. We further introduce Verus-Bench, a benchmark with fine-grained human annotations of perceptible artifacts for evaluating artifact detection. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that Verus-Insight achieves strong performance in both fine-grained artifact analysis and AI-generated video detection, with substantial gains in recovering human-perceived artifacts. Further analyses reveal that the three capabilities are complementary yet distinct, and that Verus-Insight more reliably converts relevant inspection targets into supported artifact evidence without increasing spurious artifact claims.
evidence_items.title: Verus-Insight: Towards Explainable Artifact Detection in AI-Generated Videos

evidence_items.summary: Robots must act under physical and social constraints while adapting to changes in their environment and human needs. Existing embodied-agent systems often focus on specified goals or abstract execution into symbolic actions, limiting evaluation in an evolving world. We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for physically and socially grounded long-horizon embodied agents. TARSphere-Infra runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue. An event-driven finite-state machine (FSM) uses completed actions and delivered information to update task states and evaluate outcomes. TARSphere-Harness, its embodied brain harness, lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) act through multi-level executable skills, using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback to revise its decisions. On this foundation, agent-in-the-loop curation aligns task semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry to construct TARSphere-Bench: 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes. Five paired conditions assess perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding for navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks. Our evaluation of 8 MLLMs shows that general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult. Frequent collisions and falls further motivate evaluating execution safety alongside task success, even with a shared action interface and decision budget.
evidence_items.title: TARSphere: A Robot-Oriented Full-Stack Framework for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents in Evolving Physical and Social Environments

evidence_items.summary: Code-based video generation offers fine-grained control, targeted editing, and component reuse compared with direct video generation. This approach requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to translate visual and temporal requirements into executable programs that produce complete videos. However, existing code-based benchmarks primarily target specialized tasks, leaving complete video creation across diverse creative categories and input modalities insufficiently evaluated. We introduce Code2Video-Compass, a general-purpose benchmark for code-based video generation across text-to-video (T2V), image-to-video (I2V), and video-to-video (V2V) settings. Code2Video-Compass comprises 2,104 tasks spanning 10 categories, 24 subtypes, and three complexity dimensions covering construction, dynamic animation, and state dependency. It combines tasks curated from textual instructions and visual references with corresponding T2V, I2V, and V2V tasks derived from complete professional and user-created videos. We propose a dual-level evaluation framework combining 12 objective metrics and five subjective metrics. Objective evaluation covers operational performance, video quality, text-video alignment, and reference fidelity, while subjective evaluation uses an MLLM judge to evaluate instruction following and holistic video quality. Extensive evaluation of 15 recent proprietary and open-weight MLLMs from nine families reveals that even leading models face challenges in reliably generating high-quality complete videos aligned with textual and visual requirements, with performance generally declining as construction, dynamic animation, and state-dependency complexity increases. We anticipate that Code2Video-Compass will advance reliable, coherent, and controllable code-based video generation and inspire broader progress in programmatic visual creation.
evidence_items.title: Code2Video-Compass: A Comprehensive Benchmark for General-Purpose Code-Based Video Generation across T2V, I2V, and V2V

evidence_items.summary: Effective test-time personalization requires LLM agents to adapt to query-dependent user preferences from lightweight interaction. We study persona selection with binary comparisons between candidate responses as the online signal. We present ID-TAP, a scalable, IDS-inspired neural dueling-bandit framework for large discrete persona spaces. ID-TAP combines a query-conditioned neural utility model with a lightweight Bradley-Terry explorer, and transfers comparison evidence across related queries through similarity-weighted warm starts. The neural model shares statistical strength across queries while preserving query-specific scores, and efficient BT updates score hypothetical challengers. Across seven user-conditioned generation benchmarks under reference- and model-based preference simulators, ID-TAP achieves the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated baselines within a fixed ten-round comparison budget. These results support information-directed challenger selection as an effective design for test-time persona adaptation.
evidence_items.title: Bridging Exploration and Persona: Information-Directed Dueling for Test-Time Agent Personalization

evidence_items.summary: Improving every agent in an LLM-based multi-agent system can be prohibitively costly, making it important to identify which agent should be prioritized to achieve the greatest system-level gain with limited resources. Failure attribution can inform this decision, but an agent's responsibility for failures does not directly reveal the system-level gains achievable by improving it. We therefore introduce IF-MAP, an influence-function-inspired method for identifying agents with high potential for system-level improvement. For each agent, IF-MAP measures end-to-end loss changes under controlled semantic prompt perturbations, fits a regularized local response model in a low-dimensional prompt-embedding subspace, and uses the estimated response norm as a priority score. This black-box procedure requires no access to model parameters or gradients and produces agent priorities that can guide subsequent improvement effort. We evaluate IF-MAP across six multi-agent workflows spanning code generation, question answering, and mathematical reasoning, using the same priorities for prompt optimization and model upgrades. Optimizing the selected agents' prompts achieves a macro-average gain of 3.81 percentage points, compared with 1.85 for uniform agent selection. Across five target models, upgrading the selected agents yields macro-average gains of 7.62-16.42 percentage points, compared with 3.81-8.62 for uniform agent selection. Despite its probing overhead, IF-MAP reduces Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V3.2 token use by 74.2% and 35.2%, respectively, relative to optimizing every agent, and reduces target-model tokens by 63.6-64.9% relative to upgrading every agent. These results support the use of IF-MAP to identify promising agents and direct improvement effort toward greater end-to-end performance gains.
evidence_items.title: IF-MAP: Influence-Function-Inspired Agent Prioritization in Multi-Agent Systems

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise for generalist robotic manipulation, but their inference cost remains a major bottleneck for real-time control. This limitation is especially pronounced in flow-matching VLAs such as π_{0.5}, where the action expert is evaluated repeatedly during iterative denoising. We introduce MambaAct, an efficient Mamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained visual-language prefix encoder of π_{0.5}, while replacing its transformer-based action expert with a compact Mamba-based action expert. Within this expert, Mamba serves as the action mixer that models dependencies across the noisy continuous-action sequence. To preserve visual-language conditioning without repeated token-level cross-attention, MambaAct uses a lightweight Context Compressor to map Vision-language model (VLM) prefix tokens into a compact conditioning signal that gates and modulates each Mamba action block. MambaAct uses a 10times smaller action expert and reduces flow-matching denoising latency by 64.8% on LIBERO and 58.8% in real-world deployment, while improving mean LIBERO success by 1.08 percentage points across three independent fine-tuning seeds and maintaining gains on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks. Our code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/giakhuyendihoc/MambaAct.
evidence_items.title: MambaAct: Efficient Mamba Action Experts for Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Multimodal large-language-model (LLM) evidence pipelines often attach rule-derived outcomes to candidate remediation actions even though only the executed action yields a factual production outcome. Treating those counterfactual rules as ground truth can miscalibrate routing, while discarding them wastes structured operational knowledge. We introduce EviRoute-DR, a disagreement-reliability routing method that learns when rule priors fail and combines corrected-rule experts with direct factual outcome experts through a reliability-conditioned meta-learner. The study uses 2,100 production cases, seven candidate actions per case (14,700 case-action records), and exactly one observed production outcome per case. Base models are trained on 600 factual cases, combined on 200, and evaluated on 1,300 held-out factual cases spanning main, temporal-labelled, hard, and workflow-shift cohorts. On factual outcomes, EviRoute-DR achieves AUC 0.926 and Brier score 0.0910, compared with 0.921/0.0971 for direct logistic regression and 0.924/0.0922 for a random-forest baseline. The paired bootstrap Brier improvement over logistic regression is 0.0060 (95\% CI 0.0021--0.0092). A separate production-derived counterfactual replay shows a stronger cost-resolution frontier at moderate operating costs, reaching approximately 0.815 resolution near 12 cost units. Because the logged action is always the argmax of the production score vector, we do not interpret those scores as stochastic propensities and make no inverse-propensity, doubly robust causal, or production-effect claim. The results support disagreement-aware reliability fusion as a practical methodology for evidence routing under partial factual feedback.
evidence_items.title: Disagreement reliability routing for multimodal large language model evidence pipelines with imperfect counterfactual priors

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objective This study aimed to compare the clinical quality of responses provided by four current large language models (LLMs) to orthopaedic patient questions based on expert evaluations and to investigate whether expert-rated response quality could be predicted using natural language processing (NLP), semantic representation, and machine learning methods. Materials and Methods Fifty patient-oriented questions covering anterior cruciate ligament injuries (n = 15), meniscal tears (n = 15), and total knee arthroplasty (n = 20) were submitted to ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, and Gemini, yielding 200 unique responses. All responses were independently evaluated by three orthopaedic specialists for Accuracy, Completeness, and Misinformation, generating 600 expert evaluations. Models were compared using paired statistical methods overall and at the clinical-category and question levels. NLP features were extracted from the responses, and semantic representations and question-response similarities were calculated using SBERT. An RBF-SVR model combining NLP, semantic, and explainable textual features was developed to predict response-level quality scores obtained by averaging the ratings of the three experts. To prevent data leakage, the four LLM responses to the same clinical question were kept within the same cross-validation fold, and final performance was evaluated using nested grouped cross-validation. Results The four LLMs achieved generally high Accuracy (3.607–3.827/4) and Completeness (3.633–3.780/4) scores and low Misinformation scores (0.093–0.127/2). Descriptively, Claude had the highest mean Accuracy (3.827 ± 0.288), whereas DeepSeek had the highest Completeness (3.780 ± 0.283) and the lowest Misinformation score (0.093 ± 0.243). However, no overall statistically significant differences were detected among the models for Accuracy (p = 0.070), Completeness (p = 0.361), or Misinformation (p = 0.451).
evidence_items.title: Predicting Expert-Rated Quality of Large Language Model Responses to Orthopaedic Patient Questions Using Computational Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background In Indonesia, people with communication disorders predominantly communicate using Bahasa Isyarat Indonesia (BISINDO). Nevertheless, all current systems for BISINDO recognition generate fragmented, word-by-word output and lack natural language generation (NLG) capabilities, thereby fundamentally constraining their communicative utility. Objective The aim of this study is to develop, validate, and field-evaluate SmartGlove BISINDO, an AI-assisted wearable sign language–to-speech system that embeds large language model (LLM)–powered NLG into a BISINDO translation pipeline for the first time. Methods This study followed the design science research (DSR) framework, covering phases 1 through 5 (problem identification, solution objectives, prototype design and development, demonstration, and evaluation). Data were collected from 12 purposively selected informants (6 domain experts and 6 deaf education companions/teachers) across 3 Indonesian cities (Malang, Surabaya, and Makassar), using a needs-analysis questionnaire and an expert validation sheet, and analyzed through statistical triangulation of agreement percentage, content validity ratio (CVR), and Aiken V. The validated prototype was field-tested in Makassar and Malang with 15 participants with communication disorders and 4 observers or companions; it was evaluated by a disability expert in Surabaya. Results The needs analysis yielded a grand mean of 4.77 (SD 0.51) across 4 clusters, with 89% mean agreement, indicating very high priority for all identified needs. The prototype’s 5-layer architecture integrates wearable sensors, on-device gesture classification, and LLM-based NLG. Expert validation showed an overall Aiken V of 0.94, with all 14 items exceeding the 0.75 validity cutoff and with 11/14 items (79%) rated highly valid (V>0.90).
evidence_items.title: The SmartGlove BISINDO Wearable Sensor and Large Language Model–Based Sign Language–to-Speech System for Users With Communication Disorders: Design Science Research Study

evidence_items.summary: Moral evaluation depends not only on what people do, but on why observers believe they acted as they did. Although motive inference has long been recognized as central to moral judgment, moral motivation itself has rarely been conceptualized as a multidimensional psychological representation. We investigated whether observers infer four distinct moral motivational dimensions (Approach Good, Avoid Bad, Approach Bad, and Avoid Good) from natural-language narratives and whether this representational structure is recovered by frontier large language models (LLMs). Human participants (N = 1,031) and 23 frontier LLMs evaluated 344 real-world moral narratives using identical procedures. All four motivational dimensions were inferred frequently in both populations and exhibited structured patterns of co-occurrence. Human observers clustered antisocial motivations (Approach Bad and Avoid Good) more strongly than prosocial motivations, whereas LLMs exhibited the opposite pattern. Across all evaluative outcomes, inferred motivations systematically predicted judgments of rightness, wrongness, praiseworthiness, and blameworthiness. Supervised machine learning analyses further demonstrated that the complete four-dimensional representation consistently outperformed every reduced two-dimensional alternative, indicating that each motivational dimension contributed unique predictive information. Although LLMs broadly recovered the multidimensional structure observed in humans, they inferred antisocial motivations less frequently, concentrated those attributions within fewer narratives, and produced systematically compressed response distributions characterized by lower variance and entropy. Together, these findings suggest that moral motivation is best understood as a multidimensional representational system and that representational richness provides a useful framework for evaluating both human moral cognition and its approximation by artificial systems.
evidence_items.title: Humans and Large Language Models Infer a Multidimensional Structure of Moral Motivation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate and evaluate patient-facing medical materials. Through persona prompting, LLMs can be instructed to simulate responses from individuals with different demographic and experiential backgrounds, offering a scalable approach for approximating patient feedback. However, it remains unclear how closely these simulated persona-based responses reflect real patient perspectives, and whether this alignment is consistent across demographic subgroups. Objective This study assessed whether contemporary LLMs can simulate diverse patient perspectives on hospital discharge summaries when prompted with personas defined by education, gender, and health care use. We further examined whether persona-based simulation performance was equitable across subgroups by comparing LLM-generated responses with responses from a general-population human cohort under a standardized evaluation framework. Methods We evaluated 4 contemporary LLMs, GPT-4.1, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Opus 4.6, against responses from 99 participants recruited through Prolific (Prolific Academic Ltd). Participants answered 10 questions for discharge summaries that varied in length and medical complexity. Questions included information-based items assessing factual comprehension and perception-based items assessing subjective understanding. Model-human alignment was measured using modal mean absolute error and expected absolute ordinal distance. We also conducted a chain-of-thought sensitivity analysis for cases with the greatest divergence between LLM-generated persona and matched human responses. Results Across LLMs, persona responses aligned more closely with human responses on information-based items than on perception-based items.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models’ Simulation of Patient Comprehension of Discharge Summaries: Multimodel Evaluation Study

evidence_items.summary: Importance: Patients increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) for health-related conversations, but evaluation measures largely reflect clinician judgment. Objective: To develop and preliminarily evaluate a patient instrument assessing the quality of patient-AI health conversations. Design: Cross-sectional survey conducted June 5-14, 2026, following patient-partnered instrument development and cognitive interviews. Setting: An anonymous online survey. Participants: A convenience sample of adults with prior use of large language models for personal health-related queries, recruited from an academic medical center-affiliated Insight Panel and patient peers. Exposures: Participants' own prior health-related conversations with AI tools of their choosing. Main Outcomes and Measures: The Patient-AI Rating instrument comprised 12 communication-quality and patient engagement items rated from 1 to 5 and a separately scored patient-perceived-harm item. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach alpha, with sensitivity analyses using first ratings only for those using the tool to rate multiple conversations and participant-mean profiles. We examined item-total correlations, inter-item structure, and between- and within-participant variation. Results: Fourteen participants contributed 46 complete ratings; among 13 providing demographics, median age was 63 years (IQR, 53-70 years), and 8 (62%) reported female gender. Participants provided a median of 2 ratings (range, 1-17). Cronbach alpha was 0.88 (95% CI, 0.83-0.93) across all ratings, 0.85 using first ratings only, and 0.92 using participant-mean profiles. Corrected item-total correlations ranged from 0.42 to 0.72; mean inter-item correlation was 0.40. No item deletion improved Cronbach alpha. The mean quality score was 4.43 (SD, 0.45). Among 9 participants contributing multiple ratings, the intraclass correlation coefficient was 0.45, suggesting inter-conversation variability.
evidence_items.title: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of the Patient-Artificial Intelligence Rating Instrument

evidence_items.summary: The rapid ubiquity of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally disrupted traditional pedagogical frameworks in engineering education, necessitating a critical examination of its impact on cognitive development and knowledge retention. This longitudinal study spans 30 years (1996–2025) to analyse shifts in student learning curves within an AI curriculum, testing the hypothesis that reliance on automated tools exacerbates a ‘J-curve’ learning style, characterised by delayed engagement and terminal production spikes, at the expense of fundamental understanding. By comparing weekly topic acquisition and final assessment data across cohorts, the research reveals a distinct morphological transformation from the classic sigmoidal progression (‘S-curve’) of the baseline 1996 class to an exponential ‘J-curve’ in the 2025 cohort. While modern students demonstrate high procedural efficiency in project delivery, this shift correlates strongly with a significant decline in independent examination performance, where mean scores fell from 9.50 to 7.75. Although a gradual decline in performance was observed prior to 2020, the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent ubiquity of generative AI tools may have intensified this trend (main finding). The data indicate that students utilise AI to bypass the cognitive friction necessary for deep learning, resulting in a failure to exit the assisted phase of skill acquisition. These findings suggest that current AI integration acts as a mechanism for cognitive offloading rather than scaffolding, creating a trade-off between immediate output and long-term declarative competence. The study concludes that engineering curricula must rigorously re-evaluate assessment strategies to ensure that the efficiency of automated generation does not erode the foundational logic required for sustainable innovation.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence: Learning Flow in 30 Years

evidence_items.summary: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has become an important research direction because intelligent systems are increasingly used to support decisions in complex and uncertain environments. However, the interpretability of a decision depends not only on the final prediction but also on the mathematical structure through which the prediction is obtained. This paper develops an algebraic framework for interpretable multi-criteria decision-making based on bounded ordered structures, weighted aggregation, and explicit criterion-level contributions. A finite set of alternatives is evaluated using normalized criteria, and a weighted score is assigned to each alternative. The framework represents criterion values in a bounded lattice and uses an order-preserving aggregation operator to obtain transparent rankings. Mathematical properties concerning monotonicity, boundedness, score decomposition, and stability under perturbations are established. An illustrative numerical example involving the selection of an artificial intelligence model demonstrates how the framework generates rankings and human-readable explanations. The approach provides a mathematically explicit foundation for decision support and can be extended to fuzzy, linguistic, and neutrosophic environments. The proposed framework and numerical example are illustrative; novelty and performance claims require literature verification and empirical validation. Keywords: Abstract algebra; lattice theory; explainable artificial intelligence; multi-criteria decision-making; interpretable decision systems; weighted aggregation.
evidence_items.title: Algebraic Structures for Explainable Artificial Intelligence and Decision-Making Systems

evidence_items.summary: Background. Knowledge-graph models can rank existing drugs for a disease, but their benchmarks mostly reward rediscovering known treatments, and their scores rarely come with evidence a researcher can check. We built OREVID, an open tool that shows a ranked candidate only when an evidence line supports it and reports how often each line was right on held-out data, and compared it with TxGNN on identical data. Methods. The graph combines PrimeKG, Open Targets, STRING and PubTator3 (157,822 nodes, 9.46 million edges). For each disease, 22 degree-weighted metapath features feed a LightGBM LambdaRank model trained with masked neighbourhoods. A candidate is shown only if it is indicated for an ontology-neighbour disease or for a disease sharing at least 3 associated genes (hypergeometric p &lt; 10⁻⁵ over the genes with at least one associated disease). The acceptance criteria for these rules were set in advance; the rules were revised on the hidden-treatment benchmarks and then measured on an external set of approvals not used to choose them. TxGNN was retrained with its official code on the same PrimeKG splits, and all tasks and predictions are released as OREVID-bench. Results. Zero-shot Recall@100 (mean ± SD over five splits) was 0.811 ± 0.042 for OREVID, 0.412 ± 0.042 for TxGNN and 0.358 ± 0.040 for a popularity baseline, with OREVID ahead on every split (paired difference with TxGNN 0.399, 95% CI 0.352–0.443, resampling diseases). On nine disease areas held out it was 0.617 against 0.237, ahead in all nine, although TxGNN had the higher AUPRC in five. Training OREVID without validation labels and excluding diseases where TxGNN outputs constant scores gave 0.809 against 0.421.
evidence_items.title: OREVID: Open, Evidence-Based Drug Repurposing with a Benchmark Against TxGNN

evidence_items.summary: We present a computational benchmark for large Dirichlet eigenvalue spectra on triaxial ellipsoids, comparing finite-element discretizations combined with ARPACK, inertia-based spectrum slicing (SLEPc/MUMPS), a stretched spectral Galerkin (SSG) method, and a multi-probe block-Hankel filter diagonalization that we extend here from a landmark detector into a gap-free complete-spectrum solver. Rather than ranking methods by runtime alone, we ask whether the resulting spectra preserve reliable geometric information. The unit ball serves as a quality-assurance case, since its eigenvalues are known in closed form; for the triaxial case a=1, b=1.5, c=2.3 we add a reverse-geometry validation based on the three-term Weyl law, reconstructing volume, surface area, and integrated mean curvature from finite spectral segments. As the eigenvalue index grows, the error is increasingly dominated by the mesh rather than by the eigensolver. SSG gives the strongest geometric consistency in our tests, reconstructing the volume to about 0.025%. The block-Hankel method extended by a Weyl-equal-count tiling, an analytic one-sided bandpass, and coprime decimation voting produces a complete ordered spectrum of 2034 levels including multiplicities; spectrum slicing returns the same 2034 levels on the identical matrices in 4.9 core-hours against roughly 69,400. For this task, the established method is therefore superior by four orders of magnitude, and we report that plainly. What the comparison establishes instead is agreement; three unrelated solvers on one discretization coincide to a median relative deviation of 3×10−11, with Sylvester inertia counts certifying the level count exactly. On the unit ball, where degeneracies reach 2ℓ+1=51, the certified spectrum reproduces the exact level count without deviation up to λ=600 and resolves degeneracies up to 35.
evidence_items.title: Hearing Ellipsoids: A Benchmark of Krylov, Spectral Galerkin, and Filter Diagonalization Eigensolvers
